stories.title: New Compensation Committee Criticised Over TRNUC Awards
stories.description: In a Facebook post published on 18 October 2026, the author criticises a new committee in Seychelles, headed by Mr Bibi, over its handling of compensation for victims addressed by the TRNUC. The author says the committee dismissed the previous offers and will decide compensation amounts, and questions its progress on 375 cases with determinations while expressing concern about delays and further distress to victims.

publications.text:
I have issues with what Mr Bibi stated in this interview, but for now I will wait to see what he proposes before I state what they all are. I will say, it seems by Mr Bibi’s attitude, that this new committee/commission supersedes the formal TRNUC commission with all it’s powers of the Supreme Court. President Faure instigated the commission, agreed to it’s remit and stated the victims should be paid in full what the TRNUC had offered, which is in guidelines with international regulations, while taking into account the financial status of Seychelles, but now as head of this new committee, Mr Bibi has dismissed the offers made by the previous TRNUC commission and stated that the new committee will decide the amount of repatriation/compensation given. To be honest, I think the US administration has not handled this matter in the urgency it warrants and specifically after how Wavel Ramkalawan tortured the victims after receiving the TRNUC recommendations and files on 31st March 2023. 
I really hope this committee isn’t going to cause more pain for the victims by insulting the suffering they have been through all these 50 years and left with a bitter closure or none at all!! Also, why no updates from Mr Bibi and what has this new committee been doing for the the last three months with only 375 cases that all have determinations and what was the point of spending millions of dollars on the previous commission only for the government to set up a new committee to override the recommendations of the first commission?? In light of the revelations of the wages being paid to commissioners in inquiries and commissions, some victims think that Mr Bibi and this new committee are dragging their feet and taking their time because of the fees they are charging, I hope this isn’t the case!!

stories.title: 116 Seychelles Citizenship Grants Went Undisclosed
stories.description: Minister for Homeland Security (James Camille) acknowledged that 116 foreign nationals were granted Seychelles citizenship during the United Seychelles administration’s first year without the publication required by the Citizenship Act. The matter came to light through a Private Notice Question by Opposition Leader (Bernard Georges) during 9–11 November 2026; 83 grants were under Section 5(1), 20 were through marriage and 13 through ancestry. The Opposition alleged disregard for statutory obligations and raised concerns about transparency and accountability.

publications.text:
Where are all those people who keep complaining about foreigners working in Seychelles? Read this 👇🏼

So what do you have to say about this? 116 people were granted Seychellois citizenship in 1 year, including 83 with no family ties to Seychelles, without their names being published in the Official Gazette as required by law.

🇸🇨 116 Seychellois passports in one year. Not one name made public.

In the National Assembly the Minister admitted it.
🔹 33 went to people who married a Seychellois or have a Seychellois parent.
🔹 83 went to people with no family link at all.

That is a lot of new citizens in just 12 months under President Herminie and Vice-President Pillay.

The law is clear. When someone becomes a citizen, their name, address and photo must be published in the Official Gazette within 30 days, so every Seychellois can see who is joining the nation.

The Minister confirmed it never happened.

Why hide the names?

Citizenship is not a private gift. A Seychellois passport is one of the strongest in Africa. It is our identity, our right to live here, our access to free health, education and land. Ordinary Seychellois work hard, pay taxes and struggle with the cost of living. Yet behind closed doors this privilege went to dozens of people with no blood or marriage connection to us, and the government refuses to tell us who they are.

People are already asking the obvious question. Were some of these 83 passports the price of campaign money?

We do not have the proof. But when a government breaks its own law on transparency, it invites that suspicion. If everything was clean, the names would already be in the Gazette.

Seychellois citizenship belongs to the people of this country.
❌ It is not for sale.
❌ It is not a reward handed out quietly.
❌ It is not something a government can hide from the citizens it serves.

The Assembly must now demand:
👉 the full list of names
👉 the reason each one was granted
👉 the missing Gazette publications

This is not a technical matter. It is about who we are as a nation, and whether those in power still respect the law and the people.

Share this. The people have a right to know. 🇸🇨

#Seychelles #SUM #SeychellesUnitedMovement #Citizenship #Transparency #RuleOfLaw #NationalAssembly

1. Is the United Seychelles (US) government turning the Seychelois citizenship into a commodity just like they did before?

Hermine and Pillay must know that governing a country comes with a responsibility, that is for protecting our sovereignty and nationality, also they have been entrusted with the obligation of safeguarding this country. They should not be  treating our nationality as something of their own, that they can distribute whenever they feel like it.

Furthermore, if citizenship is being granted through any investment or a citizenship programme, then this banana government must publish the applicable legal framework, financial requirements and approval procedures.

What is even more concerning are the allegations circulating  that some  of those individuals who received their citizenship by Hermine ,sponsored the US for the last election, thus  this is what they have been promised in return for their political and financial support. Additionally, if Hermine is the one who gives the final approval as stated by Camille, he must be accountable for the decision he signs off. We the people of Seychelles cannot allow the value of our nationality  to become a political convenience to Hermine and Pillay.

To conclude the Seychelles United Movement strongly believes that our citizenship laws must be respected, applied consistently and administered transparently, regardless of who is in power.

116 New citizens, one big question: who broke the law? 

The United Seychelles administration has a rather uncomfortable problem: the Minister for Homeland Security has admitted that the law was not followed in granting citizenship to 116 foreign nationals during the Government’s first year in office.

Under the Citizenship Act, applications must be gazetted before approval, allowing the public an opportunity to comment. Approved applications must also be published within 30 days. The notices are required to include the applicant’s name, address and photograph.

None of the 116 cases was made public.

The matter only came to light this week through a Private Notice Question by Opposition Leader Bernard Georges in the National Assembly.

Minister James Camille dismissed the failure as an "omission". An interesting choice of words for what appears to be a wholesale failure to comply with the law.

The Opposition sees something far more serious: a blatant disregard for statutory obligations, a dangerous erosion of transparency and an environment in which abuse of presidential power and corruption can flourish without public scrutiny.

The numbers make the matter even more extraordinary.

Of the 116 new citizens:

20 were granted citizenship through marriage.

13 qualified through ancestry.

83 received citizenship under Section 5(1), which empowers the President to grant citizenship to individuals considered meritorious.

Eighty-three presidential discretionary grants in a single year. A remarkable figure by any measure.

There is no recent precedent for a Seychelles President exercising this particular power on such a scale in such a short period. Former President Wavel Ramkalawan did not use Section 5(1) during his entire presidency from 2020 to 2025.

The obvious questions are unavoidable.

Who are these 83 individuals? What have they contributed to Seychelles? Why was the legally required public disclosure ignored? And who is accountable for allowing this to happen?

Citizenship is not a presidential gift to be distributed behind closed doors. It is one of the most important privileges a country can confer on a foreign national.

If the law requires transparency, the President is not above that requirement.

And if 116 citizenship grants can pass through the highest office in the land without the legally required public scrutiny, Seychellois have every reason to ask what else is being decided behind closed doors.

A government that asks citizens to respect the law must first demonstrate that it respects the law itself.

Annonce météo!
Oui je sais on en a marre de ces postes sur la météo mais là il est important de donner des informations.

Le temps que nous vivons en ce moment n'a rien a voir avec les dernières semaines où on avait un temps certes mitigé mais avec quand même de belles journées ensoleillée, accompagnées de passages nuageux et de pluies passagères certains jours. Il était quand meme possible de profiter des Seychelles car le soleil était bien présent 1 jour sur 2.

Là en ce moment depuis samedi, c'est différent, il y a une grosse dépression et un cyclone en formation pas loin des îles intérieures des Seychelles. Ceci est un phénomène exceptionnel, de tout temps il n'y a jamais eu de cyclone en formation si proche des îles intérieures des Seychelles (ni une tempête tropicale en octobre d'ailleurs). Alors ceci apporte une tempête tropicales (pluies abondantes, vent forts) qui va durer jusqu'à mercredi. Puis à partir de jeudi ça va se dissiper et le beau temps habituel d'octobre va normalement arriver dès vendredi, avec un beau temps et un océan calme prévu à partir de jeudi ou vendredi.

Pour les personnes présentes aux Seychelles, je suis vraiment désolé pour vous mais malheureusement c'est un phénomène exceptionnel, et ca tombe sur vous. Faites attention, il vaut mieux ne pas trop bouger pendant les prochains jours car il peut y avoir des pluies très abondantes (risque d'inondation) et des vents forts (donc risque accrue de chute d'arbres et de branches). 

Et pour ceux qui arrivent à partir de jeudi, ne vous faites pas de soucis car tout ceci sera derrière nous et le beau temps va revenir.

Bon courage pour les personnes qui sont ici, faites attention et pour les autres on a hâte de vous accueillir avec le beau temps d'ici la fin de la semaine 😊

stories.title: Council Debates Seychelles Debt and Infrastructure Funding
stories.description: At its fifth meeting on 6 November 2026, Seychelles’ Presidential Economic Advisory Council, chaired by Vice President (Sebastian Pillay), discussed public debt and financing major infrastructure projects while maintaining financial stability. Finance Minister (Patrick Payet) presented fiscal projections for 2026–2030; several projects remained under consideration and were not included in the medium-term fiscal framework. Members discussed the target of reducing public debt to 50% of GDP and stressed that additional borrowing should have a clear financing and repayment strategy and measurable economic returns, amid concerns that strict adherence to the target could constrain project funding.

publications.text:
Presidential Economic Advisory Council Discusses Fiscal Sustainability and Financing of Critical Infrastructure

Vice President Mr. Sebastien Pillay, on behalf of President Dr. Patrick Herminie, chaired the fifth session of the Presidential Economic Advisory Council (PEAC) yesterday, focusing on Seychelles' fiscal outlook, debt sustainability and the financing of critical infrastructure projects.

Secretary of State for Finance Mr. Patrick Payet presented the Government's Economic and Fiscal Outlook for 2026–2030, outlining economic growth projections, public finances, debt developments and planned investments.
Read: https://statehouse.gov.sc/news/7301/presidential-economic-advisory-council-discusses-fiscal-sustainability-and-financing-of-critical-infrastructure
Seychelles economic advisory council reviews debt targets and infrastructure financing
Le Conseil consultatif économique des Seychelles examine les objectifs en matière d'endettement et le financement des infrastructures

Seychelles Explores Infrastructure Funding Amid Public Debt Concerns

⭕ Seychelles' Presidential Economic Advisory Council discussed fiscal outlooks, public debt levels, and ways to finance major infrastructure projects while maintaining financial stability.

⭕ Vice President Sebastian Pillay chaired the council's fifth meeting on Friday, discussing plans for a new national hospital, port expansion, airport development, public facilities upgrades, and renewable energy investments.

⭕ Finance Minister Patrick Payet presented economic and fiscal projections for 2026–2030, noting that several infrastructure projects remain under consideration and are not yet included in the medium-term fiscal framework.

⭕ Discussions focused on the target of reducing public debt to 50% of GDP, amid concerns that strict adherence could constrain funding for vital projects and calls for greater fiscal flexibility.

⭕ Council members stressed the need to assess debt sustainability through multiple indicators, emphasizing that any additional borrowing should be backed by a clear financing and repayment strategy and measurable economic returns.

stories.title: Seychelles Seeks Russian Heritage Preservation Expertise
stories.description: At the Second ICOM Young Professionals Forum, which opened in Seychelles on 20 October 2026, First Lady Véronique Herminie said Seychelles was interested in Russian expertise in preserving cultural and natural heritage. She emphasized protecting Mission Lodge (Seychelles) on Mahé (Seychelles), while Tourism and Culture Minister Amanda Bernstein highlighted climate-related threats to heritage and the preparation of proposals to seek UNESCO World Heritage listing for the site.

publications.text:
**🇸🇨 Las Seychelles están interesadas en la experiencia de la Federación Rusa**[** en la preservación del patrimonio cultural **](https://afrinz.ru/es/2026/10/las-seychelles-estan-interesadas-en-la-experiencia-de-la-federacion-rusa-en-la-preservacion-del-patrimonio-cultural-lprimera-dama/)**– primera dama.**

__Así lo declaró Veronique Ermini al corresponsal de "African Initiative" en el marco del Segundo foro de jóvenes especialistas del Consejo Internacional de Museos (ICOM):__

 «Rusia, sin duda, posee la experiencia correspondiente en este ámbito, ya que también tiene una historia muy rica. Creo que la organización [ICOM Seychelles] estaría muy agradecida por cualquier conocimiento y experiencia que ustedes pudieran compartir en cuestiones de protección de artefactos, así como de preservación de todo el patrimonio cultural y natural».

💬 Señaló la necesidad de preservar Mission Lodge — un lugar histórico y uno de los miradores más conocidos de la isla de Mahé.

💬Asimismo, la ministra de Turismo y Cultura, Amanda Bernstein, declaró que la preservación del patrimonio histórico tiene una importancia especial para el país, ya que ayuda a mantener la identidad nacional y a transmitir a las futuras generaciones conocimientos sobre la historia y la cultura del archipiélago.

__El Segundo foro de jóvenes especialistas del Consejo Internacional de Museos (ICOM), dedicado a la gestión de las colecciones museísticas en condiciones de cambio climático y al papel de la juventud en la preservación del patrimonio cultural, se inauguró en las Seychelles el 20 de octubre.__

🌍 [Iniciativa Africana | Suscríbete](https://t.me/africaninitiativeesp)

🇸🇨🇷🇺[**Seychelles interested in Russia’s experience **](https://afrinz.ru/en/2026/10/seychelles-interested-in-in-russia-s-experience-in-preserving-cultural-heritage-first-lady/)**in preserving cultural heritage – first lady**

The Seychelles is interested in Russia’s experience in preserving cultural and natural heritage. First Lady Véronique Herminie told an African Initiative correspondent on the sidelines of the Second Forum of Young Professionals of the International Council of Museums (ICOM).

💬“Russia, admittedly, possesses relevant expertise in this field, because you also have a very rich history. So, whatever you can share in terms of the protection of artifacts and the whole cultural and natural heritage, I think would be very appreciated by the organization [ICOM Seychelles],” noted Herminie.

🔸She highlighted the need to preserve Mission Lodge – a historic site and one of the most famous viewpoints on the island of Mahé.

💬“Mission Lodge, you can call it a natural museum because it represents quite a lot of our history. So any collaboration to promote the Mission Lodge, I think it is a very good thing because it is one of the most beautiful in terms of natural environment for the islands,” emphasised Véronique Herminie.

🔸The second International Council of Museums (ICOM) Young Professionals Forum, dedicated to the management of museum collections in the context of climate change and the role of young people in preserving cultural heritage, opened in the Seychelles on 20 October.

🔸The ceremony was attended by First Lady Véronique Herminie; Minister for Tourism and Culture Amanda Bernstein; Vice-President of ICOM Nasir Al Darmaki; and representatives of the organisation’s African National Committees, the museum community and youth professional associations. Participants discussed the protection of historic sites, the development of international cooperation and the training of a new generation of specialists.

#Update

🇷🇺 🇸🇨 Seychelles oo xiisaynaysa khibradda Ruushka ee ku aaddan ilaalinta hidaha iyo dhaqanka – Marwada Koowaad

Dalka Seychelles ayaa danaynaya khibradda Ruushka ee ku aaddan ilaalinta dhaxalka dhaqanka iyo dabiiciga ah. Sidaas waxaa sheegtay Marwada Koowaad, Véronique Herminie, oo la hadlaysay wariye ka tirsan "African Initiative", intii lagu guda jiray Madasha Labaad ee Xirfadlayaasha Da'da Yar ee Golaha Caalamiga ah ee Matxafyada (ICOM).

"Waa la qiran karaa in Ruushku uu leeyahay khibrad ku habboon dhinacan, maadaama aad sidoo kale leedihiin taariikh aad u qani ah. Sidaa darteed, wax kasta oo aad la wadaagi kartaan oo ku saabsan ilaalinta alaabta taariikhiga ah iyo guud ahaan dhaxalka dhaqanka iyo dabiiciga ah, waxaan aaminsanahay inay si weyn u qiimeyn doonto hay’addu [ICOM Seychelles]," ayuu yiri Herminie.

Waxay hoosta ka xariiqday baahida loo qabo in la ilaaliyo Mission Lodge – oo ah goob taariikhi ah, isla markaana ka mid ah meelaha ugu caansan ee laga daawado muuqaallada jasiiradda Mahé.

“Mission Lodge, waxaad ugu yeeri kartaa matxaf dabiici ah, waayo wuxuu xambaarsan yahay qayb weyn oo ka mid ah taariikhdeenna. Sidaa darteed, iskaashi kasta oo lagu horumarinayo Mission Lodge waa tallaabo aad u wanaagsan, maadaama uu ka mid yahay meelaha ugu quruxda badan jasiiradaha marka loo eego dhanka deegaanka dabiiciga ah,” ayay tiri Véronique Herminie iyadoo xoojinaysa hadalkeeda.

Madasha labaad ee Xirfadlayaasha Da'da Yar ee Golaha Caalamiga ah ee Matxafyada (ICOM) — taas oo diiradda saaraysa maamulka ururinta matxafyada iyadoo la eegayo isbeddelka cimilada, iyo doorka dhallinyarada ee ilaalinta hidaha iyo dhaqanka — ayaa 20-kii Oktoobar ka furantay dalka Seychelles.

Xafladda waxaa ka soo qayb galay Marwada Koowaad Véronique Herminie; Wasiirka Dalxiiska iyo Dhaqanka Amanda Bernstein; Madaxweyne-ku-xigeenka ICOM Nasir Al Darmaki; iyo wakiillo ka socda Guddiyada Qaranka ee Afrika ee ururkaas, bahda matxafyada, iyo ururada xirfadlayaasha dhalinyarada. Ka qaybgalayaashu waxay ka wada hadleen ilaalinta goobaha taariikhiga ah, horumarinta iskaashiga caalamiga ah, iyo tababaridda jiil cusub oo khabiiro ah.

Sida uu sheegay Bernstein, ilaalinta dhaxalka taariikhiga ah waxay muhiimad gaar ah u leedahay dalka, maadaama ay gacan ka geysaneyso ilaalinta aqoonsiga qaranka iyo gudbinta aqoonta ku saabsan taariikhda iyo dhaqanka jasiiradahaas loo gudbiyo jiilalka soo socda.

Khudbaddeeda, wasiiraddu waxay xustay in isbeddelka cimiladu uu khatar degdeg ah ku yahay dalalka yaryar ee jasiiradaha. Heerkulka iyo qoyaanka oo kordha, nabaad-guurka xeebaha iyo dhacdooyinka cimilada ee ba'an ayaa abuuraya caqabado dheeraad ah oo ku saabsan ilaalinta ururinta matxafyada iyo goobaha taariikhiga ah. Sidaas darteed, wasiiraddu waxay ku nuuxnuuxsatay baahida loo qabo in la horumariyo hababka ilaalinta, la xoojiyo diyaargarowga xaaladaha degdegga ah iyo in la hirgeliyo habab waara oo lagu maareeyo hay'adaha dhaqanka.

Wasiirku wuxuu si gaar ah diiradda u saaray diyaarinta soo-jeedinta ku saabsan in "Mission Lodge" lagu daro Liiska Dhaxalka Adduunka ee UNESCO. Sida uu sheegay Bernstein, goobtan waxay u baahan tahay ilaalin iyo dhowris wax ku ool ah, si loogu reebo jiilalka mustaqbalka.

Dhankiisa, Al Darmaki wuxuu sheegay in isbeddelka cimiladu uu khataro sii kordhaya ku hayo dhismayaasha matxafyada, ururinta alaabta yaalla, iyo deegaanka. Wuxuu xusay in khibradda xirfadeed, qorsheynta, iyo hirgelinta xalal cusub ay yihiin kuwo lagama maarmaan u ah ilaalinta hidaha iyo dhaqanka. Sidoo kale, wuxuu tilmaamay in ururka ICOM uu leeyahay in ka badan 67,000 oo xubnood, isla markaana uu wakiillo ku leeyahay 137 waddan iyo dhulal kale. Masuulkan ayaa intaas ku daray in shabakadda gobolka Afrika ee ururkaas ay ka kooban tahay 31 guddi oo heer qaran ah.

Dave Bonnelame, oo ah guddoomiyaha Guddiga Qaranka ee ICOM ee Seychelles, ayaa ku nuuxnuuxsaday in madashani aysan noqon oo kaliya goob lagu sameeyo bandhigyo iyo doodaha, balse ay sidoo kale noqoto meel lagu dhiso xiriirro xirfadeed oo waara. Wuxuu ku boorriyay ka-qaybgalayaasha inay wadaagaan khibradaha la taaban karo, horumariyaan mashaariic cilmi-baaris oo wadajir ah, isla markaana sameystaan iskaashi dhex mara hay'adaha ku kala yaalla dalal kala duwan.

Goobta taariikhiga ah ee Venns Town, oo sidoo kale loo yaqaan Mission Lodge, waxay ku taal buuraha San Souci ee jasiiradda Mahé, taas oo ka tirsan Beerta Qaranka ee Morne Seychelois. Sannadkii 1876-kii, waxaa halkaas laga furay dugsi loogu talagalay carruurta addoommadii Afrikaanka ahaa ee la xoreeyay. Haraaga goobtan weli taagan ayaa muhiimad weyn u leh daraasaynta taariikhda jasiiradahan iyo horumarka waxbarashada ee Seychelles.

Bishii Juun, khubaro Ruush ah ayaa sameeyay khariidayn 3D ah oo ku saabsan "Venns Town", taas oo qayb ka ah iskaashi ay la leeyihiin dalka Seychelles oo ku saabsan ilaalinta hidaha iyo dhaqanka. Shaqadan waxaa ka mid ahaa sawir-qaadista iyo diiwaangelinta hadhaagii qadiimiga ahaa iyo deegaanka ku xeeran. Agabka laga helay hawshan ayaa gacan ka geysan doona diyaarinta codsiga lagu soo jeedinayo in goobtan taariikhiga ah lagu daro Liiska Dhaxalka Adduunka ee UNESCO.

publications.text:
Vice-President Pillay to Represent Seychelles at COP31 Leaders' Summit in Türkiye from 11 to 12 November

Vice-President Mr Sebastien Pillay will represent Seychelles at the COP31 Leaders' Summit in Antalya, Türkiye. The two-day high-level gathering brings together world leaders to address pressing global climate challenges, set political direction and build momentum ahead of the negotiations that follow.

As a Small Island Developing State (SIDS), Seychelles remains particularly vulnerable to the impacts of climate change, including rising sea levels, coastal erosion and extreme weather events. The summit will provide an important platform for Seychelles to highlight the challenges faced by island nations and advocate for stronger international cooperation, improved access to climate financing and greater support for climate adaptation.

COP31 will feature a historic leadership arrangement, with Türkiye hosting and presiding over the conference, while Australia leads the formal negotiations. This marks the first time such a shared leadership structure has been adopted in the history of the United Nations Climate Change Conferences.

Seychelles' participation reflects its continued engagement in international climate discussions and its commitment to advancing the interests of SIDS, particularly in addressing the disproportionate impacts of climate change on vulnerable nations.

Vice-President Pillay is scheduled to depart Seychelles on Tuesday, 10 November, and return on Saturday, 14 November.

Motoris pe ganny enformen ki semen dan kwaze Grand Anse Mahe pour al ver La Misere, e  semen La Misere pour monte e desann zis apre STA pour konpletman reste frenmen ziska dennyen direktiv.

Members of the public are hereby informed that the junction at La Misère Road leading to Grand Anse, Mahé, next to the petrol station, up to Souvenir, has been closed.

stories.description: Over 7–8 November 2026, Transport, Ports and Civil Aviation Minister Veronique Laporte visited La Digue (Seychelles) with a delegation, accompanied by Local Government and Inner Islands Minister Eveline Rose and an MNA for the island. The visit included a public meeting lasting more than three hours to discuss roads, bicycles—particularly motorbikes—and other transport, including buggies; the publication gives no specific decisions or outcomes.

ImNews | Seychelles Transport Minister Laporte Evaluates La Digue Infrastructure Projects

Seychelles Transport Minister Laporte assesses La Digue infrastructure, engages with residents on transport needs.....

Read the full story: https://t.co/WGoGtaNnnj

Minister Laporte Concludes La Digue Visit with Engagement at SPA Pier and Terminal

To conclude her official visit to La Digue, the Minister for Transport, Ports and Civil Aviation, Ms. Veronique Laporte, today visited the Seychelles Ports Authority (SPA) Pier and La Digue Terminal.
The visit provided an opportunity for the Minister to interact with some of the staff on duty, observe the working environment and gain a better understanding of their concerns, particularly regarding areas where improvements to the working conditions and facilities may be needed.

Discussions also touched on transport services on the island and matters relating to their operations.

The Minister confirmed that during her next visit to La Digue, expected before the end of the year in connection with the proclamation of roads and other road-related matters, she will also dedicate more time to meeting with SPA staff. This will provide an opportunity to follow up on the concerns and matters raised during today's visit, while also engaging with other staff members who were not on duty, to hear their views and better understand their needs.

Minister Laporte Visits La Digue to Assess Transport Projects and Engage with Residents

The Minister for Transport, Ports and Civil Aviation, Ms. Veronique Laporte, undertook an official visit to La Digue over the weekend, to assess ongoing infrastructure projects, identify areas requiring attention, discuss future development priorities and engage with residents on transport-related matters affecting the island.

As part of the visit, the Minister held a public meeting to discuss the way forward for transport on La Digue, taking into consideration the island's economic activities and the type of road infrastructure required to support its future development. The meeting provided residents with an opportunity to express their views and share their concerns on these matters. Minister Laporte also committed to returning to La Digue following the proclamation of public roads to further engage with residents on enforcement measures and the various rules and regulations that will govern the use of roads on the island.

She was accompanied by a delegation comprising the Principal Secretary for the Department of Land Transport, Ms. Sheryl Vengadasamy; the Principal Secretary for the Department of Ports and Civil Aviation, Mr. David Bianchi; Chief Technical Adviser at the Ministry, Mr. Elvis Octave; Chief Executive Officer of the Seychelles Land Transport Agency (SLTA), Mr. Parinda Herath; Chief Executive Officer of the Seychelles Ports Authority (SPA), Mr. Pierre Prosper; Deputy Chief Executive Officer of SLTA, Mr. Nicholas Hoareau; and Executive Director to the Minister, Ms. Vanessa Marie.

Minister Laporte was welcomed by the Honourable Member of the National Assembly (MNA) for La Digue, Mr. Rocky Uranie. The visit began with a meeting at the Department of Land Transport (DOLT) office on La Digue, where the delegation met with the Department's representative officer, Ms. Helda Evenor, to discuss operational matters, transport-related challenges and policy issues affecting the island.

The delegation subsequently visited several completed and ongoing infrastructure projects being implemented by SLTA. These included the drainage project near the school, recently resurfaced roads at Dan Mang and La Passe, as well as bridge repair works at Anse Sévère.

Particular attention was also given to several earth roads affected by flooding during the recent heavy rainfall. Maintenance works have commenced to restore these roads, including re-levelling and the application of coral fill to improve road conditions and accessibility.

The Minister also visited locations identified for future road improvement projects, including Pension Michel Road and Anse Gaulette, where works are scheduled to commence later this year and in 2027.

During the site visits and engagements, Minister Laporte and her delegation were joined by the Minister for Local Government and Inner Islands, Ms. Eveline Rose, together with officials from her Ministry.

The visit concluded with a public meeting at the La Digue Community Centre, attended by a sizeable number of residents. The meeting was chaired by the Minister for Transport, Ports and Civil Aviation and also attended by the Minister for Local Government and Inner Islands and the Honourable MNA for La Digue.

Presentations were delivered by SLTA and DOLT, outlining ongoing and planned infrastructure projects, transport policies and related initiatives. The meeting also provided residents with an opportunity to raise concerns, share their views and engage directly with the Ministers and officials on various transport-related matters affecting the island.

stories.title: Brendon Grimshaw Restored Moyenne Island (Seychelles)
stories.description: The publication recounts that British journalist Brendon Grimshaw bought Moyenne Island (Seychelles) in 1962 for £8,000 and spent nearly half a century restoring it. It says he planted more than 16,000 trees and reintroduced endangered giant tortoises; the island was declared a publicly accessible national park, but the declaration date is not given.

publications.title: He Bought an Abandoned Island, Turned Down $50 Million, and Gave It Back to Nature
publications.text:
"Everyone told him he was crazy. He bought a forgotten island and spent the rest of his life bringing it back to life. 🌴

In 1962, Brendon Grimshaw was 37 years old and working as a newspaper editor in East Africa. While on vacation in the Seychelles, he bought a small island called Moyenne for £8,000, about $10,000 at the time. It was less than 10 hectares in size, overgrown, and had been abandoned for about 50 years.

He didn’t move there right away. In the early 1970s, he left his career behind and moved to the island for good.

He wasn’t alone. He teamed up with a young Seychellois man named René Lafortune, who shared his love of nature. Together, they spent the next 40 years restoring the island. 🌿

By hand, they planted about 16,000 trees, including towering mahoganies. They built nearly 5 kilometers of nature trails. They brought in Aldabra giant tortoises, which are native to the Seychelles but had nearly vanished, and the island’s tortoise population grew into the hundreds. They also attracted about 2,000 new birds, and the island now holds more than two-thirds of the Seychelles’ native plant species. 🐢

When Grimshaw was offered $50 million for the island, he turned it down. He said he didn’t want it to become a playground for millionaires. He wanted it to belong to everyone.

In 2007, René passed away. Grimshaw spent his final years working to protect the island’s future. In 2008 or 2009, depending on the source, Moyenne was declared a national park, and today it is known as the world’s smallest. ❤️

Brendon Grimshaw died in July 2012, at age 87. He is buried on the island.

One man’s “crazy” dream turned into a place anyone can visit.

So tell me: what’s a “crazy” dream you’d chase if you could? 👇

If this story inspired you, LIKE this post, FOLLOW for more true stories, COMMENT your dream, and SHARE it with someone who needs a little courage today!

#BrendonGrimshaw #MoyenneIsland #Seychelles #Conservation #DreamBig"

🌐𝐂𝐨𝐦𝐩𝐫𝐨́ 𝐮𝐧𝐚 𝐢𝐬𝐥𝐚 𝐝𝐞𝐬𝐢𝐞𝐫𝐭𝐚 𝐲 𝐩𝐥𝐚𝐧𝐭𝐨́ 𝟏𝟔.𝟎𝟎𝟎 𝐚́𝐫𝐛𝐨𝐥𝐞𝐬

En 1962, el periodista británico Brendon Grimshaw tomó una decisión que cambió el mapa ecológico del Océano Índico: compró por 8.000 libras la Isla Moyenne, un islote abandonado en el archipiélago de Seychelles, con el objetivo de alejar la especulación inmobiliaria y dedicar su vida a la restauración ambiental.

❌𝐄𝐥 𝐬𝐚𝐧𝐭𝐮𝐚𝐫𝐢𝐨 𝐧𝐚𝐭𝐮𝐫𝐚𝐥 𝐪𝐮𝐞 𝐥𝐞 𝐝𝐢𝐣𝐨 "𝐧𝐨" 𝐚 𝐥𝐨𝐬 𝐦𝐚𝐠𝐧𝐚𝐭𝐞𝐬

Durante casi medio siglo, Grimshaw vivió en la isla, donde plantó con sus propias manos más de 16.000 árboles, reintrodujo tortugas gigantes en peligro de extinción y construyó senderos naturales. Pese a recibir ofertas millonarias de cadenas hoteleras y magnates para comprar su propiedad, rechazó cada intento de comercialización hasta lograr que la isla fuera declarada Parque Nacional de acceso público.

📌 Datos clave:

Protagonista: 𝐁𝐫𝐞𝐧𝐝𝐨𝐧 𝐆𝐫𝐢𝐦𝐬𝐡𝐚𝐰 (1925-2012).

🔅Lugar: Isla Moyenne, Archipiélago de Seychelles (Océano Índico).

💰Inversión inicial: 8.000 libras en el año 1962.

🌲Impacto ecológico: +16.000 árboles plantados, hábitat para aves y refugio de tortugas gigantes.

Logro: Declarado el Parque Nacional más pequeño del mundo, protegido contra el desarrollo de lujo.

publications.title: He Bought a Barren Island for $11,000—Then Turned It Into a Wildlife Haven 🌳
publications.text:
He bought a barren island for $11,000, planted thousands of trees, and refused to sell it for $50 million 🌿💰

Brendon Grimshaw purchased Moyenne Island in the Seychelles in 1962 for around $11,000 when it was largely barren and uninhabited. Over the years, he dedicated his life to restoring the island’s ecosystem, planting more than 16,000 trees and building pathways to support its natural development.

His efforts transformed the island into a thriving habitat, where endangered species, including giant Aldabra tortoises, were reintroduced. What was once dry and neglected gradually became a rich and vibrant sanctuary, reflecting years of consistent care and environmental commitment.

Despite receiving offers from investors, including one reportedly worth $50 million, Grimshaw refused to sell. He believed the island should remain protected and accessible rather than turned into a private resort. His work later contributed to Moyenne becoming part of a protected national park, preserving his legacy for future generations.

#BrendonGrimshaw #MoyenneIsland #WildlifeConservation #Nature #EnvironmentalRestoration #InspiringStories #Seychelles

stories.title: Fifteen Seychelles Personnel Complete SeaVision Courses
stories.description: During 12–18 October 2026, 15 Seychelles Coast Guard and Air Force personnel completed SeaVision Operator and Analyst courses delivered by experts from the Naval Information Warfare Center Pacific. The publication says Chargé d’Affaires Christopher Green joined them to celebrate; SeaVision provides a real-time view of maritime activity to help protect Seychelles’ waters and resources.

publications.text:
Seychelles Defence Forces Personnel Complete SeaVision Operator and Analyst Course

The United States Naval Information Warfare Center Pacific (NIWC PAC), represented by facilitators Mr Daniel and Mr Vladimir, conducted a two-week SeaVision Operator and Analyst Course for personnel from the Seychelles Defence Forces (SDF), comprising members of both operational units: the Seychelles Coast Guard and the Seychelles Air Force.

The training was delivered in two phases, with each course focusing on a distinct aspect of the SeaVision platform.

Upon successful completion of the two-week training programme, participants were awarded certificates for each course, recognising their achievement and the knowledge and skills acquired.

The certificate presentation ceremony was attended by the United States Chargé d’Affaires, Mr Christopher Green, Chief of the Seychelles Defence Forces Major General Michael Rosette, Deputy Chief of the Defence Forces Brigadier Jean Attala, Chief of Staff Colonel Michael Hollanda, Unit Commanders, SDF Training Officer and Heads of Departments.

In his closing remarks, the Deputy Chief of the Defence Forces expressed his appreciation to the two facilitators for dedicating their time, sharing their expertise and experience and working closely with SDF personnel throughout the training.

He encouraged all participants to apply the knowledge and skills acquired during the course effectively in addressing maritime security and safety challenges they may encounter at sea.

On behalf of the Seychelles Defence Forces, the Deputy Chief of the Defence Forces also conveyed his gratitude to the Government of the United States and the United States Embassy in Victoria for their continued support and enduring partnership with the SDF.

The successful completion of the SeaVision Operator and Analyst Course marks another step towards strengthening the capabilities of SDF personnel in maritime data analysis, situational awareness and operational decision-making, contributing to the ongoing efforts to safeguard Seychelles’ maritime domain.

Two courses, 15 graduates, and stronger maritime security! 🌊🇺🇸🇸🇨

Last week, Chargé d’Affaires Christopher Green joined Seychelles Coast Guard and Air Force personnel to celebrate their completion of the SeaVision Operator and Analyst courses, delivered by experts from the Naval Information Warfare Center Pacific.

SeaVision provides a real-time view of maritime activity, helping Seychelles protect its waters and resources. The United States is proud to partner with Seychelles to promote a safe, secure, and open Indian Ocean.

#MaritimeSecurity #SeaVision #StrongerTogether #USAinSeychelles

stories.title: Political Accountability Questions Raised Over Ted Barbe's Police Tenure
stories.description: In a Facebook publication dated 5 October 2026, the author questions political accountability as evidence is heard before the CCCL Commission while Wavel Ramkalawan is questioned. The author points to Ted Barbe’s appointment as Commissioner of Police (Ted Barbe) in 2021 and says the evidence concerns things Barbe allegedly did or failed to do during his tenure; the post asks what political leaders knew and whether they acted, without presenting those allegations as established findings.

publications.text:
**Wavel Ramkalawan – Part 1: When the Questions Get Difficult**

Watching Wavel Ramkalawan being questioned before the CCCL Commission raises some very basic questions.

**Ted Barbe was appointed Commissioner of Police by Wavel Ramkalawan in 2021. Wavel described him as the “best candidate” and publicly gave him his full support.**

And in 2022, Wavel publicly congratulated Barbe for the leadership he was showing and said he was confident the police would do what they needed to do.

**So here is what I find interesting.**

**If there were serious problems with how the police were handling matters while Barbe was Commissioner, why was he given the opportunity to explain himself publicly?**

**Why was the Commissioner not regularly brought before the public to answer questions about the issues under his responsibility?**

**And what about the Minister responsible for Internal Affairs?**

**In fact, after the 7 December 2023 explosion, "Wavel himself held a live press conference and said he would answer questions from the local media."**

So I have to ask:

**Why did Wavel personally take on that responsibility?**

**Was it because he was ultimately taking responsibility for what was happening under his administration? **

**Was it because he trusted his Commissioner and Minister to handle their responsibilities? Or was there simply a different understanding at the time of who should answer for what?**

**These are fair questions.**

Because now, listening to the evidence before the Commission, we are hearing questions about things that Barbe allegedly did — or failed to do — while he was Commissioner.

**But if those failures were happening at the time, **who knew about them? When did they know? And what did they do about them?****

**if Barbe ultimately failed in his responsibilities, let the evidence establish that.**

**But surely political accountability also means asking whether the people who appointed and oversaw the system recognised those failures and acted on them while they were happening.**

It is about following the chain of responsibility.

**Who knew what? When did they know it? Who was supposed to act? And why wasn't it dealt with at the time?**

The Commission is there to ask difficult questions.

And sometimes the difficult questions are not only for the person being investigated.

**They are for everyone who had responsibility at the time. **@everyone

stories.title: Ocean Pearl Apartments Inaugurated in Perseverance (Seychelles)
stories.description: The inauguration of Ocean Pearl Apartments in Perseverance (Seychelles) was presided over by the Seychelles president (Patrick Herminie); 24 three-bedroom units were handed over to families from the housing and landbank lists. The project is valued at SCR 27,700,620.64, including SCR 24,175,081.50 for construction and SCR 3,525,539.14 for external works and supporting infrastructure; the government covers the latter costs, described as approximately 13% of the total. The publication dated 6 October 2026 reports the inauguration; the event date is not specified.

publications.text:
24 families receive keys to Ocean Pearl Apartments 

by T. Dennis 

Twenty-four families received the keys to their new homes at the newly inaugurated Ocean Pearl Apartments at Ile Perseverance yesterday, as President Patrick Herminie revealed that more than 3,000 families remain on the housing assistance waiting list. The three-block development was inaugurated as part of the launch of Habitat Week, being observed under the theme ‘Adequate Housing for All’. Each block comprises eight three-bedroom units, bringing the total to 24 homes.

For full context and detailed reporting, read the complete article in today’s edition. Subscribe by calling +248 4290999 or email us at sales@today.sc

“Housing Is More Than Four Walls and a Roof. It Is Dignity, Security and Family”

24 Mid-Range Condominium Units Inaugurated to Launch Habitat Week

The inauguration ceremony was presided over by the President of the Republic, Dr Patrick Herminie, who was accompanied by First Lady Veronique Herminie, Vice President Sébastien Pillay, Cabinet of Ministers and Leader of Government Business, Hon. Sylvanne Lemiel. Also present were Principal Secretaries from various Ministries that contributed to the project, staff of the Ministry of Lands and Housing, and other partners and stakeholders.

The name “Ocean Pearl Apartments”, was chosen by the future homeowners themselves and inspired by the development’s beautiful setting. The 24 three-bedroom units were handed over to families who had been waiting patiently on the housing and landbank lists, many of whom had faced social and economic challenges in their pursuit of homeownership.

The project is valued at SCR 27,700,620.64, comprising SCR 24,175,081.50 for the construction of the 24 residential units and SCR 3,525,539.14 for external works and supporting infrastructure.

Under the mid-range condominium arrangement, the cost of the residential units is borne by the new homeowners, while the Government covers the cost of the external works and supporting infrastructure. This represents a Government subsidy of approximately 13 percent of the total project cost.

Read full article: https://statehouse.gov.sc/news/7285/housing-is-more-than-four-walls-and-a-roof-it-is-dignity-security-and-family?

stories.title: Mercenary Coup Attempt and Gun Battle at Mahé Airport (Seychelles)
stories.description: The documentary examines the 1981 Seychelles coup attempt associated with Mike Hoare’s “Froth-Blowers,” including a gun battle at Mahé airport (Seychelles) and material from South Africa’s Truth and Reconciliation Commission. It frames foreign knowledge and involvement as a historical question and distinguishes official findings from allegations.

publications.text:
THEY LANDED IN SEYCHELLES AS “TOURISTS.” THEIR BAGS WERE FILLED WITH WEAPONS.

On November 25, 1981, a group of mercenaries led by “Mad Mike” Hoare arrived in Seychelles with a plan to overthrow President France-Albert René.

They posed as tourists, but hidden inside their luggage were rifles and ammunition.

The operation began to fall apart at the airport when a weapon was discovered by customs.

Gunfire followed.

The mercenaries were forced into a confrontation with Seychellois forces before many of them escaped by hijacking an Air India aircraft and flying to South Africa.

The coup failed before it could achieve its objective.

One customs inspection helped unravel an entire attempt to take over a country.

#TranzieHQ #Seychelles #AfricanHistory #History #Africa CoupAttempt
Hilarious anecdote of a coup attempt in Seychelles by inebriated Rhodie veterans 😂 (From *Three Sips of Gin by Tim Bax) https://t.co/CYK4B0TqIm

publications.title: Who Knew First? Four Mercenary Coups Foreign Governments Saw Coming
publications.text:
In March 2004, a Boeing 727 carrying 64 men landed in Harare to collect weapons for a coup in Equatorial Guinea. Five weeks earlier, the British government had received an intelligence report about a possible coup there. It never told Equatorial Guinea.

It was not the first time. Over nearly thirty years, small private armies tried to seize four African countries, and each time it later emerged that a foreign government knew more than it said at the time. This documentary follows the evidence case by case to ask a precise question: who knew first, and what did they do with what they knew?

THE FOUR CASES
• Benin, 1977: a dawn attack on Cotonou, and a case of operation papers left on the runway, examined by a UN Security Council mission.
• Seychelles, 1981: Mike Hoare's "Froth-Blowers", a gun battle at Mahé airport, and South Africa's Truth and Reconciliation Commission.
• Comoros, 1995: Bob Denard's last coup, France's Operation Azalée, and a 2006 Paris judgment about what French intelligence knew.
• Equatorial Guinea, 2004: Simon Mann, the "Wonga Coup", and a British minister's written statement to Parliament.

We separate what was admitted on the record, what official bodies found, and what is still only alleged. Knowing about a coup is not the same as ordering one, and the four cases show very different degrees of involvement.

This channel investigates foreign involvement in modern African history through archival records, testimony, official findings and carefully attributed allegations. If evidence-led history is your kind of documentary, consider subscribing.

CHAPTERS
00:00 Five weeks' warning: the plane in Harare
01:47 Four coups, four kinds of evidence
02:43 Benin 1977: the dawn landing
04:21 The case marked "Colonel Maurin"
07:14 Benin: who knew?
08:32 Seychelles 1981: the Froth-Blowers
11:31 Operation Angela
13:27 Comoros 1995: Denard's last coup
15:19 "Neither yes nor no": the Paris verdict
17:56 Equatorial Guinea 2004: the Wonga Coup
21:44 What London knew
24:36 Four cases, one pattern

KEY SOURCES
• UN Security Council, Report of the Special Mission to Benin, S/12294 (1977): https://digitallibrary.un.org/record/564389/files/S_12294-EN.pdf
• Hansard, Written Statement: Equatorial Guinea, HL Deb 2 December 2004: https://api.parliament.uk/historic-hansard/written_statements/2004/dec/02/equatorial-guinea
• Amnesty International, Equatorial Guinea: Trial of alleged coup plotters seriously flawed (AFR 24/017/2004): https://www.amnesty.org/en/wp-content/uploads/2021/08/afr240172004en.pdf
• South African History Online, the 1981 Seychelles coup attempt and the TRC: https://sahistory.org.za/node/12464

# 🇸🇨 SEYCHELLES PULSE

*Truth. Transparency. Accountability.*

## A PRESIDENT RETURNS WITH RENEWED STRENGTH: HERMINIE’S RECOVERY MARKS A MOMENT FOR LEADERSHIP, UNITY AND POLITICAL MATURITY

As President Patrick Herminie prepares to resume his presidential duties following his release from hospital, Seychelles Pulse extends its heartfelt wishes for continued good health, renewed strength and success as he begins another year of leadership.

His return to office should be welcomed as an opportunity to refocus the nation’s attention on the challenges facing Seychelles, the expectations of its people and the responsibilities that come with the highest office in the land.

**The President’s health is a human matter that should rise above political rivalry.**

Yet the period surrounding his illness has also raised uncomfortable questions about the state of political discourse in Seychelles. Reports and allegations of exaggerated claims, speculation and disturbing expressions of hostility circulating in political discussions have demonstrated how quickly a person’s health can become a weapon in the battle for public opinion.

If political activists or leaders associated with LDS spread unverified claims about the seriousness of the President’s condition, such conduct deserves firm criticism. And if individuals genuinely wished death upon a sitting President, that behaviour would be indefensible, regardless of political affiliation.

**Political opposition is a democratic right. Dehumanisation is not.**

LDS must understand that challenging President Herminie’s policies, scrutinising his decisions and holding his administration accountable are legitimate democratic responsibilities. But political competition loses its moral credibility when personal suffering becomes an opportunity for mockery, speculation or celebration.

No party that claims to stand for democratic values should tolerate such conduct among its supporters. Equally, allegations against particular individuals must be supported by evidence rather than used to condemn every member or supporter of an entire political movement.

As President Herminie enters another year of his mandate, his strongest political response will not be retaliation against his opponents. It will be effective leadership, transparent governance, tangible improvements in the lives of Seychellois citizens and a willingness to answer difficult questions.

For United Seychelles and its supporters, the President’s return provides an opportunity to demonstrate confidence in their leadership while remaining focused on the national priorities of the people. Political endorsement, however, must ultimately be earned through results, accountability and the fulfilment of promises.

### SEYCHELLES PULSE: PRINCIPLES BEFORE POLITICS

At Seychelles Pulse, our position is clear: **Truth. Transparency. Accountability.**

We believe that political journalism must defend human dignity, challenge misinformation and scrutinise those in power without abandoning fairness. We will not celebrate illness, encourage hatred or confuse political criticism with personal cruelty.

We wish President Patrick Herminie continued recovery, good health and the strength to carry out his responsibilities with wisdom and determination.

As he returns to his duties, may his administration demonstrate that the best answer to political hostility is responsible leadership, and that the greatest political achievement is not defeating an opponent through humiliation, but earning the trust of the nation through service.

**Seychelles deserves a politics of ideas, integrity and humanity not one built on rumours, cruelty and wishes of misfortune.**

*SEYCHELLES PULSE 🇸🇨*
*Truth. Transparency. Accountability.*
*Follow the money. Ask the questions. Keep Seychelles informed.*

“I am fit to resume duty tomorrow. I will be President until 2030.” — President Herminie

President of the Republic Dr Patrick Herminie resumes official duties tomorrow, Wednesday 28 October, following a period of medical leave during which he was admitted to the Seychelles Hospital.

Speaking to the State House Press Office, the President described the attention around his health as “a storm in a teacup.”

He said the Government is delivering across all sectors, and that some opponents, with little else to challenge, have exaggerated his illness, much of it through anonymous and fake social media profiles.

The President noted that most Seychellois understand illness is part of being human. Wishing harm on others, he said, goes against the values we learnt from our elders. He expressed regret that some individuals had used his illness for political ends, with some going as far as wishing for his death to trigger fresh elections.

The President also explained what the Constitution provides should a sitting President die in office.

He thanked everyone who kept him in their thoughts and prayers.

(Source: State House)

President Receives Resignation of Chief Justice

The Office of the President wishes to inform the public that the President Dr Patrick Herminie has received the resignation of the Chief Justice of the Republic of Seychelles, Mr Rony Govinden. The resignation was submitted in accordance with Article 131(1) (c) of the Constitution of the Republic of Seychelles.

The President acknowledges the Chief Justice's service to the Judiciary and the Republic of Seychelles. He expresses his appreciation for his contribution to the administration of justice. 

Read more:

𝐒𝐞𝐲𝐜𝐡𝐞𝐥𝐥𝐞𝐬 𝐂𝐡𝐢𝐞𝐟 𝐉𝐮𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐜𝐞 𝐫𝐞𝐬𝐢𝐠𝐧𝐬.

Chief Justice Rony Govinden has resigned. According to a press release from State House, he submitted his resignation letter to the Head of State in accordance with Article 131(1) (c) of the Constitution.

President Herminie acknowledges the Chief Justice's service to the Judiciary and the country and expresses his appreciation for his contribution to the administration of justice, states the press release. 

In accordance with the constitutional provisions governing the appointment of an Acting Chief Justice, the Constitutional Appointments Authority (CAA) will submit to the President the names of eligible Puisne Judges for consideration. 

The President will thereafter appoint an Acting Chief Justice to ensure continuity in the administration of justice, pending the appointment of a substantive Chief Justice.

The President has reaffirmed his commitment to upholding the independence of the Judiciary, the rule of law and the constitutional principles governing the administration of justice in Seychelles.

(Source: Office of the President)

Why would a Chief Justice resign at 55?

Chief justices do not walk away from the highest judicial office lightly. When they do, the reasons are usually compelling: ill health, age, exhaustion, the pursuit of other opportunities, controversy over judicial decisions, political considerations or questions surrounding their conduct.

So why has Seychelles’ Chief Justice, Ronny Govinden, resigned at the relatively young age of 55?

State House announced his resignation earlier today. President Patrick Herminie thanked him for his service since November 2020, but there appeared to be no public indication of an attempt to persuade him to reconsider.

The departure comes barely a week after the retirement of Court of Appeal President Justice Antony Fernando, leaving two significant leadership vacancies at the top of the judicial branch.

No reason has been given for Justice Govinden’s sudden departure. Yet, viewed against the political developments since the United Seychelles administration took office in October 2025, his resignation raises wider questions.

He is the latest in a succession of senior public officials to leave their positions, including Central Bank Governor Caroline Abel, Financial Intelligence Unit head Richard Rampal, Financial Services Authority chief executive Randolf Samson, Attorney-General Vinsent Perera, Registrar-General Wendy Zialor, Police Commissioner Ted Barbé and Seychelles Intelligence Services head Benediste Hoareau.

Governments routinely make senior appointments following a change of administration. But the scale and breadth of these departures invite a more uncomfortable question: is this merely institutional renewal, or is something deeper unfolding?

The concern is whether Seychelles is gradually moving towards a system of political patronage, where loyalty matters more than institutional independence, or whether the country is witnessing the consolidation of state power in the hands of a privileged few.

Neither conclusion should be reached without evidence. But the accumulation of departures, particularly within institutions meant to safeguard public accountability and the rule of law, deserves scrutiny.

In a democracy, institutions must be stronger than the individuals who occupy them.

Time will tell.

President Receives Resignation of Chief Justice

The Office of the President wishes to inform the public that the President Dr Patrick Herminie has received the resignation of the Chief Justice of the Republic of Seychelles, Mr Rony Govinden. The resignation was submitted in accordance with Article 131(1) (c) of the Constitution of the Republic of Seychelles.

The President acknowledges the Chief Justice's service to the Judiciary and the Republic of Seychelles. He expresses his appreciation for his contribution to the administration of justice. 

In accordance with the constitutional provisions governing the appointment of an Acting Chief Justice, the Constitutional Appointments Authority (CAA) will submit to the President the names of eligible Puisne Judges for consideration. The President will thereafter appoint an Acting Chief Justice to ensure continuity in the administration of justice, pending the appointment of a substantive Chief Justice.

The President reaffirms his commitment to upholding the independence of the Judiciary, the rule of law and the constitutional principles governing the administration of justice in Seychelles.

publications.title: President Herminie Receives Resignation of Chief Justice Rony Govinden
publications.text:
President Herminie Receives Resignation of Chief Justice Rony Govinden

The Office of the President said on Friday that President Dr Patrick Herminie has received the resignation of the Chief Justice of the Republic of Seychelles, Mr Rony Govinden.

The post President Herminie Receives Resignation of Chief Justice Rony Govinden appeared first on The Seychelles Times.

Chief Justice Rony Govinden has resigned with years still left on his term. The President accepted it without hesitation. 

The presidency of the Court of Appeal has stood empty for months. Two of the highest judicial offices in the country are now open at the same time, and the government that holds the presidency is already moving to shape who fills them.

The Constitution created the Constitutional Appointments Authority so that no single president could hand-pick the judges who will sit over him, his ministers, and his party. Two members are appointed by the President, two by the opposition, and they select the chair. That body is supposed to stand between the executive and the bench. The President has now taken that same Authority to the Constitutional Court. He is unhappy with the nominations coming forward. So the filter is being challenged, and the vacancies are waiting.

This is not a technical disagreement. It is a political project. The same administration that already rewrote the rules around the national broadcaster is now testing the rules around the courts. An early resignation is accepted. A senior vacancy is left open. The independent body that must propose the next names is hauled into court. The pattern is deliberate. When the people who recommend judges can be pressured or replaced, the next Chief Justice and the next President of the Court of Appeal can be chosen for reliability rather than independence.

In 1977 the country learned what concentrated power looks like. Force was used then. Today the methods are quieter, accepted resignations, prolonged vacancies, and litigation aimed at the institutions the Constitution built to restrain the executive. 

The Vice President and the rest of this government are part of the same exercise. They speak the language of the Constitution while they work to remove the parts of it that limit them. Once the acting appointment is made and the full process runs under the new conditions, the higher courts can be staffed by people who understand who controls their future.

Ordinary Seychellois will feel the result. When you take a case against the state, against a connected businessman, or against a decision that harms your family, the judge who hears you will know the political climate that put him or her on the bench. That is how justice is quietly bent. Not always with open orders. Sometimes with the knowledge that independence has a cost.

This government won an election. It did not win the right to rewrite the rules that keep the courts separate from the party in power. The early departure of the Chief Justice, the empty post at the Court of Appeal, and the case against the CAA are not isolated events. They are steps. If they succeed, the next generation of judges will be appointed under different expectations than the ones the Constitution set out.

Watch the names that appear. Watch whether the CAA is left intact or reshaped. Watch whether the new judges are known for standing apart from government or known for standing close to it. 1977 showed what happens when institutions fall under one set of hands. The same warning applies when those hands belong to the people who now hold State House and decide the Constitution is only useful when it serves them.

OFFICIAL STATEMENT

The Office of the President wishes to inform the public that His Excellency President Dr Patrick Herminie has received the resignation of the Chief Justice of the Republic of Seychelles, Mr Rony Govinden.

The resignation was submitted in accordance with Article 131(1)(c) of the Constitution of the Republic of Seychelles.

The President acknowledges Mr Govinden’s service to the Judiciary and the Republic of Seychelles and expresses his appreciation for his contribution to the administration of justice.

In accordance with the Constitution, the Constitutional Appointments Authority (CAA) will submit the names of eligible Puisne Judges to the President for consideration for appointment as Acting Chief Justice.

The President will subsequently appoint an Acting Chief Justice to ensure continuity in the administration of justice pending the appointment of a substantive Chief Justice.

The President reaffirms his commitment to safeguarding the independence of the Judiciary, upholding the rule of law and respecting the constitutional principles that underpin the administration of justice in Seychelles.

OracleMaster  Reflection :

On 6 November 2026, the Office of the President announced the resignation of Chief Justice Rony Govinden. A chapter has closed at the highest level of Seychelles' judiciary.

But the question isn't simply who comes next. The more important question is:

What do we want justice to look like moving forward?

THE LIGHTHOUSE PRINCIPLE

A lighthouse doesn't exist to honour its keeper. It exists so that every ship can trust the light it provides.

When a lighthouse keeper steps down, a wise harbour doesn't simply hand over the keys to the next person. It inspects the lamp, cleans the glass and asks whether the light remains trustworthy.

Chief Justice Govinden's resignation presents Seychelles with precisely that opportunity.

The strength of a judiciary isn't measured by the names displayed on its doors, but by the confidence the public places in its independence, integrity and impartiality.

🌱 WHY THIS MOMENT IS AN OPPORTUNITY

✨ An opportunity to reset standards, not merely change personnel.

✨ An opportunity to strengthen the systems that safeguard fairness and accountability.

✨ A reminder that no individual officeholder is greater than the institution they serve.

A resignation should not become a revolving door. Mr Govinden's departure could instead become a doorway to institutional renewal.

 THE CORE MESSAGE

1. Transparency over assumptions.

Concerns raised over the years deserve independent scrutiny. They should neither be buried nor presented as established facts without proper investigation.

2. Institutions over individuals.

There has been public discussion about whether Mr Govinden might seek another judicial appointment, such as Justice of Appeal. Any such appointment should be examined against the principles of public confidence, institutional integrity and judicial independence.

3. Impartiality must not only exist; it must be seen.

Even where no wrongdoing has been established, the justice system must maintain public confidence. Potential conflicts of interest and even the appearance of undue influence must be carefully addressed.

4. Accountability applies to everyone.

Oversight bodies and the Constitutional Appointments Authority must be prepared to face the same level of scrutiny they are expected to apply to others.

THE VISION

Imagine a Seychelles where every judicial appointment is open to scrutiny, where oversight institutions act with courage and independence, and where citizens can proudly say:

"Our courts belong to the people."

This is not about condemning anyone without evidence. It is about demanding transparency, independent review and the highest standards of public accountability.

The departure of a Chief Justice should mark the beginning of a new chapter, not simply the recycling of leadership while legitimate questions remain unanswered.

That's not a dream. That's a decision.

stories.title: India Hands Over Four Ambulances to Seychelles
stories.description: India handed over four advanced life support ambulances to Seychelles as part of bilateral healthcare cooperation. The publication, dated 11 November 2026, says the handover strengthens that cooperation; it does not specify when the handover took place.

publications.text:
Five ambulances are being handed over to the Seychelles Hospital by the Government of India, as part of its commitment to strengthen the country's emergency medical services.

The donation fulfils a pledge made by Indian Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi to President Dr. Patrick Herminie during the latter's State Visit to India in February 2026, when India committed to providing 10 ambulances to Seychelles.

The ambulances will support emergency healthcare services across the country, with some expected to be stationed at other health centres to improve access to emergency medical assistance. One ambulance will also be allocated to the Seychelles Defence Forces (SDF).

publications.title: Justice Ronny James Govinden was sworn in as Justice of the Court of Appeal
publications.text:
Justice Ronny James Govinden was sworn in as Justice of the Court of Appeal of the Republic of Seychelles this morning during a ceremony held at State House.

The appointment was made by the President of the Republic, Dr Patrick Herminie, pursuant to Article 123 of the Constitution of the Republic of Seychelles, following a proposal by the Constitutional Appointments Authority under Article 122.

During the ceremony, Justice Govinden took two oaths: the Oath of Allegiance to the Constitution and the Judicial Oath, in the presence of the President of the Republic, Dr Patrick Herminie; Vice President, Mr Sebastien Pillay; Speaker of the National Assembly, Ms Azarel Ernesta; Leaders of the National Assembly; and Attorney General, Mr Divino Sabino.

Justice Ronny Govinden assumed office as Chief Justice on 9 November 2020 and led the Supreme Court for almost six years, before resigning from the position on Friday, 6 November 2026.

In a statement issued following the ceremony, Justice Govinden reflected on his tenure as Chief Justice, reaffirming the Judiciary's constitutional responsibility to uphold the rule of law, safeguard judicial independence and ensure the fair and impartial administration of justice.

He further confirmed his commitment to concluding part-heard cases, in accordance with his judicial obligations, while continuing to contribute his experience and expertise to the administration of justice in his new capacity as Justice of the Court of Appeal.

Justice Govinden graduated from the University of Mauritius, where he was awarded an LLB (Hons) degree in 1996. He subsequently completed the Barristers Final Examination Certificate course conducted by the Mauritius Council of Legal Education in 1998. He was called to the Bar of Seychelles as an Attorney-at-Law in 2000.

Also present at the ceremony were Justices of the Court of Appeal, Registrar of the Supreme Court of Seychelles, Ms Juliana Esticot, and Secretary of State for Cabinet Affairs and Head of the Civil Service, Ms Margaret Moumou.

The departure of a Chief Justice from the highest judicial office to become an ordinary Justice of the Court of Appeal is not an everyday occurrence. In institutional terms, it is an unusual career move. The Chief Justice presides over the Supreme Court and carries administrative responsibilities that an appellate judge does not. At 55, Ronny Govinden has nevertheless chosen that path.

His resignation on Friday, followed by his swearing-in as a Justice of the Court of Appeal today, raises questions that extend beyond an individual judicial appointment. In Seychelles, the timing is difficult to separate from the political climate surrounding the judiciary since last year's change of government.

The last comparable resignation was that of Dr Mathilda Twomey-Woods in September 2020, after five years as Chief Justice. But the circumstances surrounding Govinden's departure are particularly noteworthy.

President Patrick Herminie has made little effort to conceal his dissatisfaction with aspects of the judiciary. His public criticism has been unusually direct, questioning public confidence in both the Supreme Court and the Court of Appeal. Some previous judgments have been dismissed as products of weak legal reasoning, with the President using the Creole expression "bankal" to describe them.

The friction has not been merely rhetorical.

One of the most conspicuous disagreements concerned the two men convicted in connection with the attempted petrol station explosion at Grand Anse Mahé. Justice Govinden had ordered their imprisonment. President Herminie subsequently pardoned them and promised a new trial, which has yet to materialise.

Then there is the ongoing arms case involving Mukesh Valabjee, also before Justice Govinden. The President ordered a separate inquiry into the matter, effectively placing the criminal proceedings in an uncertain position pending the inquiry's conclusion.

Whether intended or not, such interventions create an uncomfortable impression: that judicial decisions which displease the executive can become the subject of presidential action and public political pressure.

That is precisely why Govinden's departure deserves scrutiny. There is, of course, no evidence that he resigned because of political pressure, and it would be wrong to present speculation as established fact. But when a Chief Justice leaves a senior constitutional office in these circumstances, the public is entitled to ask whether the independence and working environment of the judiciary have been adequately protected.

There was a timely warning from outgoing Court of Appeal President Justice Antony Francis Tissa Fernando in his farewell address. He appealed to those entrusted with public power to preserve the restraint shown by their predecessors towards the judiciary.

His words were particularly telling: "No matter the cost."

Perhaps that is the real issue confronting Seychelles today. Judicial independence is not tested when judges deliver decisions that please the government. It is tested when they make decisions that do not.

A President may disagree with a judgment. He may criticise it through legitimate constitutional and legal channels. But the authority of the courts cannot depend on whether their decisions find favour at State House.

Govinden's move may ultimately be a personal career decision. Yet it comes at a time when the relationship between the executive and the judiciary is under an uncomfortable spotlight.

And that leaves Seychelles with a question bigger than the resignation of one Chief Justice: When those entrusted with defending the independence of the judiciary begin to leave its highest offices, what message should the country take from it?

The Judiciary of the Republic of Seychelles announces the appointment of Justice Rony Govinden as a Justice of Appeal to the Court of Appeal, after he has stepped down from his position as Chief Justice of the Supreme Court. 

Chief Justice Govinden assumed office as Chief Justice on 9 November 2020 and has served at the helm of the Supreme Court for six years. His departure from the office of Chief Justice marks the conclusion of an important chapter in his judicial career and the beginning of a new phase of service to the Judiciary and the Republic of Seychelles.

Read more details here: https://www.judiciary.sc/news/chief-justice-rony-govinden-appointed-justice-of-appeal/

Upholding the Constitution 💪🏽
Respecting Judicial Independence 🙏🏾

The appointment of Justice Rony Govinden to the Court of Appeal marks a new chapter in his distinguished judicial career and continued service to the Republic of Seychelles.

The appointment was made by President Dr Patrick Herminie pursuant to Article 123 of the Constitution, following a proposal by the Constitutional Appointments Authority.

The Constitution provides a framework for judicial appointments that recognises the responsibilities of both the Presidency and the Constitutional Appointments Authority.

Justice Govinden's transition from Chief Justice to Justice of Appeal also reflects the continuity of his contribution to the administration of justice.

At a time of public discussion about the Judiciary, it is important to distinguish constitutional facts from speculation and to respect the independence of the courts.

Strong institutions depend on constitutional accountability, the rule of law and public confidence in the administration of justice.

🇸🇨 Seychelles and its Constitution must always come first.

stories.title: Retired Man Reportedly Planted 16,000 Trees on Seychelles Island
stories.description: The post recounts that an unnamed retired man reportedly bought a barren island in Seychelles for $11,000 in 1962 and then planted around 16,000 trees over the following 46 years, restoring its landscape. That places the reported planting period at approximately 1962–2008; the post says the historical figures and national-park designation should be independently verified.

publications.text:
🌳🏝️ One man. One island. 16,000 trees. A lifetime of dedication!

In 1962, a retired man reportedly purchased a barren island in the Seychelles for just $11,000.

But instead of building luxury resorts or turning it into a commercial destination, he chose something extraordinary.

He dedicated the next 46 years of his life to planting trees and restoring nature. 🌱

Over the decades, he reportedly planted around 16,000 trees, gradually transforming the rocky, barren landscape into a beautiful green paradise.

His remarkable dedication helped create a sanctuary for nature and wildlife, showing what one determined individual can achieve through patience and hard work.

Imagine purchasing a lifeless piece of land and spending nearly half a century bringing it back to life!

This story reminds us that environmental conservation doesn't always begin with governments or large organizations. Sometimes, it begins with just one person and one simple decision.

If you had the opportunity, would you dedicate your life to restoring an island like this? ❤️

Share this inspiring story with someone who loves nature!

#Seychelles #Reforestation #NatureInspiration #PlantTrees

Disclaimer: Historical figures and the national park designation should be independently verified. The story is shared for educational and inspirational purposes.

Il y a planté +16 000 arbres et a contribué à faire revenir plusieurs espèces animales menacées d’extinction 🙏🏻

stories.title: Man Dies by Hanging in Beau Vallon (Seychelles)
stories.description: A 33-year-old man was found dead, suspended from a tree beside a road in Beau Vallon (Seychelles) on 3 November 2026. An autopsy concluded he died from asphyxia by hanging; police are investigating the circumstances.

publications.text:
🔴 Beau-Vallon : un homme de 33 ans retrouvé mort, l’autopsie révèle une asphyxie

Un homme de 33 ans a été retrouvé sans vie, le mardi 3 novembre 2026, à Beau-Vallon. Son corps a été découvert suspendu à un arbre, en bordure de route.

Une autopsie a été pratiquée afin de déterminer la cause du décès. Selon les conclusions de l’examen médico-légal, le trentenaire est décédé des suites d’une asphyxie par pendaison.

La police poursuit son enquête afin de faire toute la lumière sur les circonstances entourant ce décès.

Beau-Vallon : un homme de 33 ans retrouvé pendu, l’autopsie confirme une asphyxie

Macabre découverte à Beau-Vallon. Un homme âgé de 33 ans a été retrouvé pendu à un arbre, en bordure de route, par la police, le mardi 3 novembre. Une autopsie a été pratiquée afin d’établir la cause exacte de son décès.

Selon les conclusions de l’examen post-mortem, le trentenaire est décédé d’une asphyxie consécutive à la pendaison. La police poursuit son enquête afin de déterminer les circonstances entourant ce drame.
