stories.title: Draft Lobster Harvest Strategy Weighs Stock Recovery
stories.description: The article describes a draft lobster harvest strategy discussed at Savoy Hotel and Spa in Beau Vallon (Seychelles) on 13 October 2026; the proposal would use stock assessments to determine whether fishing opens, season lengths, and when fishing stops. It reports licensed fishers’ concern that a closed season does not necessarily stop others from catching lobster, and says the Seychelles Fisheries Authority recognizes that illegal catches pressure the same stocks.

publications.text:
🔵 Shaping a Sustainable Future for Seychelles’ Lobster Fishery 🦞 

The Seychelles Fisheries Authority (SFA) in collaboration with The Nature Conservancy's FishPath initiative and supported by the International Climate Initiative, today held a workshop at Savoy Resort and Spa, Beau Vallon, to present and discuss the draft harvest strategy for the lobster fishery.

Bringing together participants from Mahé, Praslin and La Digue, the workshop reviewed the findings of the 2025 lobster stock assessment, current management measures, data collection and proposed rules to guide future fishing activities.

⚠️ The findings raise concerns. The assessment indicates that the lobster stock remains overfished, with large, mature lobsters becoming increasingly rare in surveys and catches.

Participants shared valuable feedback and recommendations, including increasing patrols, strengthening enforcement against illegal fishing, exploring alternative fishing areas and using survey results to help guide the opening of future fishing seasons.

The feedback will help shape the draft harvest strategy, which aims to establish an evidence-based approach to managing the lobster fishery, protecting the resource while safeguarding the livelihoods of licensed fishers.

📊 The stock assessment will be updated using the latest 2026 fisheries data, followed by further engagement with fishers to present the updated findings and finalised strategy.

Sustainable fisheries start with sound science, effective management and collaboration with our fishing communities. 🌊

#seychellesfisheriesauthority #lobsterfishery #SustainableFisheries #FisheriesManagement #OceanStewardship

Lobster fishers weigh proposed rules for seasons and stock recovery 

by K. Doku 

For licensed lobster fishers, a closed season means waiting to earn from the resource again. It does not necessarily mean others have stopped catching it. That imbalance underlies the draft harvest strategy discussed at Savoy Hotel and Spa, Beau Vallon, on Tuesday 13 October. It would set out how assessments determine whether fishing opens, how long seasons last, and when fishing stops.
The Seychelles Fisheries Authority (SFA) acknowledges its limitation: it governs legal fishing while illegal catches pressure the same stocks.

stories.title: Seychelles Presents Proposed National Addressing System
stories.description: On 5 November 2026, the Ministry of Local Government and Inner Islands led a sensitization session for National Assembly members on the proposed National Addressing System and its preparation roadmap. CEO Neddy Padayachy outlined a proposed road-distance numbering model and postcode framework; a second presentation covered road-naming issues pending review in nine districts.

publications.text:
On Thursday 5th November 2026, Honourable Members of the National Assembly of Seychelles attended a sensitization session led by the Ministry of Local Government and Inner Islands on the proposed National Addressing System (NAS) Project, an initiative aimed at establishing Seychelles' first comprehensive national addressing framework.

The session, led by CEO Mr. Neddy Padayachy, provided Members with an overview of the project's objectives, governance structure, implementation roadmap and the progress achieved to date in preparations for a nationwide addressing system. This initiative is expected to improve postal and logistics services, strengthen emergency response capabilities, support urban planning and utilities management, and facilitate the delivery of digital government services and e-commerce activities.

Members were informed that the proposed addressing model is based on an internationally recognised metric system, whereby building numbers are assigned according to their distance from the start of a road. The system would also introduce a national postcode framework based on islands, districts and sub-district postal zones, in line with Universal Postal Union standards.

Mr. Padayachy emphasised that, “Once internationally certified, these postcodes will be universally unique and aligned with global addressing standards. This will enable Seychelles to achieve the same level of address standardisation practised internationally, creating new opportunities for service delivery, digital transformation and national development".

A second presentation was then delivered on the Road Naming status of all Districts, with Mr. Bistolet providing an overview of the 9 Districts with pending issues, omissions, and names requiring further review. These issues included repetitions in names, oversights by the NAC while mapping, and the significance of road names. Members took the opportunity to pose questions and take note of the pending issues for further follow up within their Districts with partners such as the District Administration, the NAC, as well as residents.

stories.title: East Coast Project Phase 4 Launched at Île Aurore (Seychelles)
stories.description: On 9 October 2026, the Seychelles president (Patrick Herminie) launched East Coast Project Phase 4 at Île Aurore (Seychelles), Mahé (Seychelles). The government plan covers approximately 55 hectares of reclaimed land at Île Aurore and Providence (Seychelles), with more than 1,800 homes and other developments envisioned; these are proposed benefits, not completed results.

publications.text:
HERM­INIE LAUNCHES EAST COAST MEGA-PROJECT: DEVELOPMENT AMBITION MEETS POLITICAL OPPORTUNITY FOR UNITED SEYCHELLES

By Seychelles Pulse News | 12 October 2026

ÎLE AURORE, MAHÉ President Dr Patrick Herminie has officially launched the East Coast Project Phase 4 (ECP4), marking a major milestone in Seychelles’ long-running land reclamation programme and placing housing, economic development and the country’s limited land resources firmly on the national agenda.

The launch ceremony, held at Île Aurore on 9 October, brought together senior government officials, Vice-President Sébastien Pillay, representatives of Belgian dredging company Jan De Nul and other invited guests. The project will create new land at Île Aurore and Providence, opening opportunities for residential, industrial, tourism and infrastructure development.

A PROJECT WITH NATIONAL CONSEQUENCES

The proposed reclamation covers approximately 55 hectares according to the State House announcement, with other reports giving a slightly higher estimate. Government plans envisage more than 1,800 houses, alongside schools, sports facilities, industrial areas and other developments. These are future development ambitions, not completed achievements.

For a country where mountainous terrain and limited coastal land constrain housing and business expansion, the project addresses a significant development challenge. Its ultimate value, however, will depend on whether the newly created land translates into affordable housing, productive investment, employment and infrastructure that Seychellois people can access.

President Herminie presented the initiative as an investment in future generations, emphasising the need to balance development with environmental responsibility. 

THE POLITICAL SIGNIFICANCE FOR UNITED SEYCHELLES

Beyond its engineering and economic dimensions, the launch carries political significance for President Herminie and the United Seychelles (US) party. Major infrastructure projects can become defining features of an administration’s public identity, particularly when they address issues that directly affect households and businesses.

1. Demonstrating a governing agenda

The project gives the administration a visible, long-term development initiative to communicate to the public. Housing shortages, access to land and the cost of development are concerns with direct consequences for families. By placing these issues at the centre of a national project, Herminie can demonstrate that his government has identified tangible development priorities.

For United Seychelles, this creates an opportunity to explain its governing programme through a concrete infrastructure initiative rather than relying solely on political speeches or party messaging.

1. Connecting national development with household aspirations

The promise of homes, schools, roads and business opportunities has considerable public relevance. If the project ultimately delivers these benefits fairly and efficiently, the administration will have a measurable basis on which to demonstrate progress.

For the party, the political opportunity lies in connecting national investment to improvements in everyday life. But the distinction between a promise and a delivered benefit will remain crucial.

1. Building a long-term development narrative

Land reclamation is not new to Seychelles. Earlier phases of the East Coast Project helped create areas subsequently used for housing, industry and essential infrastructure. ECP4 therefore builds on a development programme that predates the current administration.

Herminie’s political challenge and opportunity is to show how the fourth phase will respond to today’s needs and what additional value it will deliver. United Seychelles can highlight the launch as part of the government’s development agenda while recognising the historical foundations of the wider programme.

1. Engaging young people and future homeowners

The project has particular relevance for younger Seychellois who aspire to own homes, establish businesses and raise families. The President explicitly framed the initiative around the needs of future generations.

This provides the government with an opportunity to explain how land availability, housing policy, skills development and employment are connected. For United Seychelles, the strongest evidence of progress would be accessible opportunities for young people, rather than the scale of the ceremony itself.

1. Attracting investment and supporting economic diversification

The government has identified industrial land, marina facilities, tourism and residential development as potential uses for the reclaimed areas. Properly planned investment could expand economic activity and create employment opportunities.

Politically, this allows the administration to present infrastructure development as part of a wider economic strategy. The benefits will depend on investment actually materialising, jobs reaching Seychellois workers, and public interests being protected in the allocation and development of land.

THE ACCOUNTABILITY TEST: PROMISES MUST BECOME RESULTS

Despite the project’s potential, its launch should not be confused with its completion. The public will ultimately need clear answers on project costs, financing, implementation schedules, environmental safeguards and the criteria governing the allocation of reclaimed land.

Questions about who benefits from future residential and commercial developments will be especially important. If public land creates substantial private investment opportunities, the government will need to demonstrate that the wider Seychellois population also receives a fair share of the economic and social benefits.

Environmental monitoring will be equally significant. Reclamation can create new development space, but coastal ecosystems and marine resources must be protected through effective safeguards and transparent oversight.

These are not merely technical matters. They will shape public confidence in the administration and influence how the project is judged over time.

CONCLUSION: A POLITICAL OPPORTUNITY, NOT A GUARANTEED VICTORY

President Herminie’s launch of East Coast Project Phase 4 gives his administration and United Seychelles a significant national development initiative around which to communicate their priorities. Housing, land availability, employment and investment are issues that reach beyond party politics and affect the country’s long-term future.

The political advantage for United Seychelles will depend on what happens after the launch: whether construction proceeds as planned, whether costs are managed responsibly, whether land is allocated transparently and whether the promised opportunities reach ordinary Seychellois.

For now, the project represents an important step in the government’s development programme. Its lasting political and national significance will be determined not by the ceremony, but by the results delivered to the people of Seychelles.

President Herminie Launches New Land Reclamation Project to Shape Seychelles' Future

The promise of new homes, schools, businesses and opportunities for future generations took a significant step forward today as President Dr Patrick Herminie officially launched the East Coast Project Phase 4 (ECP4) at Ile Aurore, marking another chapter in Seychelles' land reclamation programme.

Upon arrival, the President received a warm welcome from students before joining dignitaries for the official ceremony.

President Dr Patrick Herminie today gave the coup d’envoi to officially launch reclamation works at Île Aurore, as the dredger performed the ceremonial scoop.
Addressing those gathered were Secretary of State for Lands, Housing and Infrastructure, Mr Joseph François; Mr Filipe Morobe, Area Director of Jan De Nul; and Mr Lablache, consultant for the project.
Across both phases, the project is expected to create more than 570,000 square metres of new land for housing, infrastructure and economic development. The wider plans for Île Aurore include 1,008 affordable housing units. 
The ceremony carried a sense of nostalgia, with patriotic songs and a journey through Seychelles’ reclamation history, reflecting on how these projects have helped shape the country we know today.

Held as part of Habitat Week under the theme “Adequate Housing for All”, today’s ceremony marks another step towards creating space for future homes and communities.

publications.text:
Africa's New Credit Rating Agency in Talks With 15 Sovereigns: Media 

AfCRA aims to publish its first ratings by March, according to interim CEO Sifiso Falala, cited by the media.

👉 Staff from the Mauritius-based agency will conduct research in countries including Togo, Kenya, Seychelles, Burundi, and Mauritius, he added.

ℹ️ Launched last month, privately owned AfCRA challenges the big three rating firms, which African leaders say overstate lending risks in Africa and downgrade countries too quickly during periods of stress.

🌍 **L’agence africaine de notation **[**publiera ses premières notes avant la fin mars 2027**](https://afrinz.ru/fr/?p=364173&preview=true)

L’Agence africaine de notation de crédit (AfCRA), créée en guise d’alternative aux grandes agences mondiales de notation, prévoit de publier ses premières notes dans plusieurs pays d’ici à la fin du mois de mars 2027. C’est ce qu’a indiqué le 3 novembre, dans un entretien à l’agence Reuters, son directeur général par intérim, Sifiso Falala.

🔸 Selon lui, les collaborateurs de l’agence sont en discussion avec quinze États, dont le Togo, le Kenya, les Seychelles, le Burundi et Maurice, en vue de réaliser des analyses.

« Nous serons en mesure, d’ici mars, avant la fin du mois de mars, d’avoir publié des résultats », a relevé Sifiso Falala.

🔸 Il a expliqué que l’approche de l’AfCRA en matière d’évaluation de la solvabilité des États devait permettre de porter un autre regard sur les économies africaines. Selon son directeur général, l’agence attribuera des notes à la demande des États eux-mêmes et mènera également des analyses sur les institutions multilatérales africaines, dont Afreximbank, et sur des établissements financiers privés.

stories.title: Seychelles Projected to Record 1.0% Real GDP Growth in 2026
stories.description: A social-media publication dated 27 October 2026 cites October 2026 IMF World Economic Outlook data, projecting Seychelles’ real GDP growth at 1.0% for 2026 and describing the tourism-heavy island economy as recovering slowly. This is a projection, not a reported realized growth outcome.

publications.text:
📉 LEAST PERFORMING AFRICAN ECONOMIES 2026.

Real-time IMF data (October 2026 World Economic Outlook)

While some African countries are among the world’s fastest-growing, others are barely moving — or even shrinking.

These projections real GDP growth in 2026:

1. 🇬🇶 Equatorial Guinea — –1.7%  

Only economy expected to contract. Declining oil production from mature fields and almost no diversification.

2. 🇸🇹 São Tomé and Príncipe — 0.4%  

Tiny island economy with high debt and very limited options beyond cocoa and tourism.

3. 🇿🇦 South Africa — 1.0%  

Biggest economy on the continent but stuck. Electricity problems, broken logistics (ports & rail), high unemployment, and weak investment.

4. 🇲🇿 Mozambique — 1.0%  

Insurgency in the north + repeated climate disasters (cyclones and floods).

5. 🇸🇨 Seychelles — 1.0%  

Tourism-heavy small island state still recovering slowly.

6. 🇱🇸 Lesotho — 1.1%  

Heavily dependent on South Africa and struggling manufacturing.

7. 🇳🇦 Namibia — 2.0%  

Soft commodity prices and fiscal pressure.

8. 🇲🇼 Malawi — 2.6%  

Forex shortages, high inflation, and climate vulnerability.

9. 🇨🇫 Central African Republic — 2.7%  

Ongoing conflict and extremely weak institutions.

10. 🇲🇺 Mauritius — 2.7%  

Mature economy facing slower tourism and financial services growth.

Poorest countries by GDP per capita (2026 IMF estimates):  

🇸🇸 South Sudan (~$488)  
🇧🇮 Burundi (~$550)  
🇨🇫 Central African Republic (~$613)  
🇲🇬 Madagascar (~$630)  
🇲🇿 Mozambique (~$635)

Main reasons behind the weak performance:  

• Over-reliance on oil or a single commodity  
• Conflict and insecurity  
• Broken infrastructure (especially power and logistics)  
• Climate shocks  
• High debt and limited policy space  

Africa’s growth is real — but it’s extremely uneven.

Which country do you think has the biggest chance of turning around?

Drop your thoughts 💬 👇

stories.title: Seychelles Seeks Russian Medical Training Cooperation
stories.description: Health Minister Marvin Nolan Fanny told African Initiative that Seychelles is interested in expanding medical cooperation with Russia, including specialist training, professional exchanges and treatment of combat-related trauma. He made the remarks on 3 November 2026 at a reception aboard the Russian frigate Marshal Shaposhnikov in the port of Victoria (Seychelles), citing the limited range of clinical cases local doctors encounter and the potential value of exchanging expertise.

publications.text:
🇸🇨🇷🇺 Seychelles interested in developing cooperation with Russia in military and civilian medicine

Seychelles is interested in expanding cooperation with Russia in military and civilian medicine, including the training of medical specialists, exchange of professional experience and treatment of traumatic injuries in combat conditions.

Health Minister Marvin Nolan Fanny told African Initiative about this on 3 November during a reception aboard the Russian Pacific Fleet frigate Marshal Shaposhnikov in the port of Victoria.

According to the minister, Seychelles has a relatively small population, which means that local doctors have fewer opportunities to encounter a wide range of clinical cases. Cooperation with countries that have greater medical resources and experience would help Seychelles specialists develop their professional skills.

Mr Fanny particularly highlighted the importance of exchanging experience between the military forces of the two countries in the fields of military medicine, battlefield medicine and trauma treatment.

The minister expressed confidence that professional exchanges could become a foundation for closer cooperation between Russian and Seychellois medical specialists.

🌍 African Initiative continues to cover the development of Russia–Seychelles cooperation.

#Seychelles #Russia #Healthcare #MilitaryMedicine #RussiaAfrica #AfricanInitiative

🇸🇨🇷🇺**Seychelles **[**interested in co-operation with Russia**](https://afrinz.ru/en/2026/11/seychelles-interested-in-co-operation-with-russia-in-military-medicine-health-minister/)** in military medicine**

Seychelles is interested in developing co-operation with Russia in military and civilian medicine, including specialist training, sharing experience in trauma treatment and providing medical assistance in combat conditions. Seychelles Health Minister Marvin Nolan Fanny told African Initiative this on 3 November at a reception aboard the Russian Pacific Fleet frigate Marshal Shaposhnikov.

🔸According to Fanny, the small population of Seychelles means that local medical professionals encounter a limited number of clinical cases. Training and exchanging experience with countries that have greater resources and larger patient numbers therefore help doctors improve their professional skills.

💬“Most of our professionals go and train overseas, at least to degree level. <…> It’s always helpful to have exposure to other nations who are more experienced in terms of the number of patients they treat. And it’s good to have exchanges, especially between our military forces, so as to learn what is currently happening in terms of military medicine, battlefield medicine and trauma,” the minister stressed.

🔸According to him, such contacts could provide a basis for closer co-operation and professional exchanges between specialists.

The Seychelles Home Care Agency (SHCA) has taken another important step towards modernising home care services with the launch of its newly developed Home Care Information System and revamped official website, during an event held at Avani+ Barbarons Hotel on Thursday, 29 October 2026.

🔗 Visit the website now: www.shca.gov.sc

The new website serves as a central platform for the public to access information on home care services, learn about the Agency’s work, and engage with SHCA through feedback, complaints, suggestions and enquiries.

The launch was graced by Vice-President Sebastien Pillay, who oversees the portfolios of Information Communication Technology, Digital Transformation and Information. In his remarks, he commended SHCA for taking the initiative to embrace digital transformation in line with the Government’s agenda to improve public service delivery.

He highlighted that the new digital system will strengthen control, facilitate faster procedures, and support fair, objective and equitable verification of information and assessment of applications. He reaffirmed the Government’s commitment to promoting transparency, good governance and higher standards of service across public entities.

Coinciding with the International Day of Care and Support, the Vice-President also paid tribute to caregivers who provide daily assistance to older persons and persons with disabilities.

On behalf of President Dr Patrick Herminie and the Government, he expressed sincere appreciation for their dedication, describing their work as a noble service that provides not only practical support but also comfort, dignity and companionship to those who need it most.

He further reassured caregivers of the Government’s commitment to improving home care services and supporting the modernisation and professionalisation of the sector. He encouraged caregivers to seize training opportunities to strengthen their knowledge and skills as the Agency advances its professionalisation plans.

Minister Pamela Charlette, whose Ministry oversees SHCA, highlighted that 2026 has been a year of transformation, marked by greater coordination and collaboration among government entities to ensure that services reach the most vulnerable in a fairer and more effective manner.

She noted that the revamped website provides an additional channel for SHCA to communicate with the community, share information about its services, and receive public feedback, complaints and suggestions.

The launch marks another step towards a more accessible, transparent and efficient home care system, placing information and services within easier reach of the people who need them.

The event also provided an opportunity for guests, partners and stakeholders to network and exchange views during a networking session following the launch.

Visit www.shca.gov.sc today and explore the new platform!

publications.text:
President Herminie Stands with Family of Missing Coast Guard Serviceman

Days after the Seychelles Defence Forces formally ended the search for two Seychelles Coast Guard servicemen missing at sea since 16 September, the President of the Republic, Dr Patrick Herminie, visited the Larue family home at Anse Aux Pins this morning to stand with the family of Denis Oreddy.

The President spent time with Mr Oredy's loved ones, including his mother and his seven-month-old daughter, offering comfort at a moment of profound grief and uncertainty.

"No family should face this alone. The Government stands by them."
President Herminie said.

The President will also visit the family of the second serviceman to extend the same support.

The thoughts and prayers of the President and the people of Seychelles remain with both families.

stories.title: Île Aurore (Seychelles) Dredging Returns to 24-Hour Schedule
stories.description: The Government says dredging for the Île Aurore (Seychelles) Land Reclamation Project is to return to its original 24-hour schedule from 10 November 2026. It says operations are now farther offshore and noise readings are within acceptable levels; monitoring will continue to minimize disruption to nearby communities, and residents of Île Perseverance (Seychelles) are thanked for their patience during the temporary adjustment.

publications.text:
Original dredging schedule to resume at Île Aurore
The Government wishes to inform members of the public that dredging operations for the Île Aurore Land Reclamation Project will return to their original 24-hour schedule from tonight, Tuesday, 10th November 2026. 
Dredging is now taking place farther offshore and noise monitoring has confirmed that readings are well within acceptable levels. Resuming round-the-clock operations will help keep the project on schedule for completion.
The project’s environmental officer will continue to monitor noise levels throughout the reclamation works to help minimise disruption to nearby communities.
The Government also thank residents of Île Perseverance for their patience and understanding during the temporary adjustment.

📢 PUBLIC NOTICE
Temporary adjustment to dredging hours

Residents of Île Perseverance are advised that dredging hours for the Île Aurore Land Reclamation Project have been temporarily adjusted following concerns about noise at night.

🕚 Dredging will stop at 11:00 pm and resume at 5:00 am daily.

This change takes effect immediately and will remain in place until the nearshore bunding works are completed.

The revised hours aim to reduce night-time disturbance while allowing the project to progress.

Thank you to residents for raising their concerns and for their continued patience and understanding.

stories.title: Patrick Herminie Hospitalised With Flu, Expected to Return
stories.description: The Seychelles president (Patrick Herminie) was reportedly hospitalized in Victoria (Seychelles) with a bad flu, according to his wife. The report was published on 26 October 2026 and said he was expected to return to his duties on 28 October 2026; the hospitalization date is unspecified.

publications.text:
President Dr. Patrick Herminie has been admitted to Seychelles Hospital for medical observation.

He is remaining in the country for monitoring and tests rather than seeking treatment abroad.

Healthcare workers are actively evaluating his health and ensuring quality care.

The president's condition is currently reported as stable while further medical tests are conducted.

BREAKING NEWS: President of Seychelles, Dr. Patrick Herminie, has been admitted to Seychelles Hospital for medical observation and tests. His condition is reported to be stable, and he remains in the country for monitoring rather than seeking treatment abroad.

President Patrick Herminie is recovering quite well from a bad flu, First Lady Veronique Herminie has written on her Facebook page.

stories.title: La Digue (Seychelles) Campaign Sterilizes 349 Cats and Dogs
stories.description: Network for Animals says its veterinary team completed its second sterilization campaign on La Digue (Seychelles); the publication dated 10 November 2026 reports the completion, but does not specify when the campaign took place. The team sterilized 349 animals—84 dogs and 265 cats, including 202 unowned community and feral cats—and says torrential rain disrupted trapping and clinic access.

publications.text:
🇸🇨🐾 LA DIGUE UPDATE: 45 ANIMALS STERILISED IN JUST TWO DAYS! 🐶🐱❤️

Our Network for Animals veterinary team has hit the ground running on La Digue, Seychelles, and we're already making a lifesaving difference for the island's dogs and cats!

After arriving yesterday, our team jumped straight into action, performing an emergency C-section and sterilisation on a mother dog in distress, as well as neutering six cats.

Today marked our first full day of surgery, with another 40 animals receiving veterinary attention!

🐾 TODAY'S IMPACT – 8 OCTOBER:

✂️ 38 cats and dogs sterilised – 22 cats and 16 dogs
🩺 One animal treated for an ear injury
💔 Sadly, one critically ill kitten rescued from the island's garbage dump was beyond help and had to be humanely euthanised to end its suffering

❤️ OUR RUNNING TOTAL SO FAR:

🐶🐱 45 animals sterilised since arriving on La Digue.
🚑 3 special veterinary cases.

That's 47 animals who have received veterinary attention in just two days!

Every sterilisation brings us one step closer to reducing the number of unwanted puppies and kittens born on La Digue, while every animal treated is a reminder of how desperately this island needs accessible veterinary care.

None of this would be possible without our generous supporters. THANK YOU for helping us bring lifesaving veterinary services to animals who need them most! 💛

We're only getting started, so keep following our daily updates!

🙏 Please donate today to help us sterilise, treat and save as many animals as possible during this campaign.
 
👉 Read more: https://zurl.co/rJOJu

🇸🇨🐾 289 ANIMALS STERILIZED AND COUNTING! OUR LA DIGUE TEAM KEEPS GOING! 🐶🐱❤️

Another day, another incredible achievement for our Network for Animals veterinary team on La Digue, Seychelles!

Despite the long hours, exhausting conditions, and challenging tropical weather we've faced during this campaign, our dedicated team continues to push forward to help as many animals as possible. 💪

🐾 TODAY'S TOTAL: 47 MORE ANIMALS STERILIZED!
🎉 CAMPAIGN TOTAL SO FAR: 289 ANIMALS STERILIZED!

That's 289 dogs and cats who will no longer contribute to the island's growing population of unwanted puppies and kittens!

Every sterilization helps break the cycle of uncontrolled breeding, reducing the number of vulnerable animals born into a life of uncertainty, hunger, and suffering.

❤️ And behind every surgery is an extraordinary team of veterinarians, veterinary assistants, and animal trappers working tirelessly to make a lasting difference for La Digue's animals.

From hiking to remote locations to reach feral cat colonies to working through tropical storms and sweltering heat, our team has refused to let anything stand in the way of helping animals in need!

🙏 To everyone supporting this campaign, THANK YOU! Your generosity is helping us bring much-needed veterinary care to animals who might otherwise never receive it.

🐱🐶 Please help us keep going! Donate today and be part of creating a kinder future for La Digue's animals.
🔗 https://zurl.co/GQGDm

🇸🇨🐾 349 CATS AND DOGS STERILIZED – OUR LA DIGUE CAMPAIGN WAS A HUGE SUCCESS! 🐶🐱❤️

After six intense surgery days, countless hours of cat trapping, torrential tropical rainstorms and a few unexpected challenges, our Network for Animals veterinary team has completed its second sterilization campaign on La Digue Island in the Seychelles!

And what an incredible achievement:

❤️ 349 cats and dogs sterilized
🐶 84 dogs – 45 females and 39 males
🐱 265 cats – 138 females and 127 males

🐾 202 unowned community and feral cats were humanely trapped, sterilized and returned to their familiar surroundings – representing an incredible 76% of all cats sterilized during the campaign.

Every sterilization means fewer unwanted litters, fewer vulnerable puppies and kittens born into hardship, and a brighter future for La Digue's cats and dogs.

It wasn't easy. Torrential rain severely disrupted our trapping operations, made it difficult for owners to bring their animals to the clinic and complicated efforts to catch roaming dogs. Several team members also suffered infected cat bites that required hospital treatment.

But our team persevered, working tirelessly to help as many animals as possible.

And the impact is already visible. On our final morning on La Digue, one of our team members spotted seven cats during a bicycle ride. Six had ear tips – a sign that they had already been sterilized ❤️

None of this would have been possible without our incredible supporters, our dedicated veterinary and trapping teams, our campaign partners Seychelles SPCA and Be Kind, and the wonderful La Digue community who welcomed us back with open arms.

THANK YOU for helping us tackle pet overpopulation, prevent suffering and create a future with fewer homeless cats and dogs on La Digue 🇸🇨❤️!

👉 Donate today to keep saving lives: https://ow.ly/Xr3f5104v4j

stories.title: Seychelles Approves Draft Tobacco-Control Amendments
stories.description: On 4 November 2026, the Seychelles National Assembly approved a draft bill to amend the Tobacco Control Act, which has been in place since 2009. All 28 members present voted in favour; the proposed amendments would regulate newer tobacco products, including electronic cigarettes and vapes.

publications.text:

Sa bann lamannman i neseser prenan kont bann nouvo prodwi taba ki’n vin lo marse e pe ganny konsonmen, parey sigaret elektronik oubyen 'vape'.

Sa bann nouvo propozisyon pe fer ki zot osi zot ganny byen regilarize e kontrole.

National Assembly passes Bill to regulate e-cigarettes and vapes

by S. Surman

The National Assembly passed the Tobacco Control (Amendment) Bill, 2026 (Bill No. 17 of 2026) unanimously on Tuesday, 3 November 2026. The Minister for Health, Dr. Marvin Fanny, presented the Bill to the House. He was accompanied by a delegation comprising the Public Health Commissioner, Dr. Jude Gedeon; Programme Manager Ms. Barathi Viswanathan; and the Principal Legal Draftsperson from the Attorney General’s Office, Mr. Victor Hill.

For full context and detailed reporting, read the complete article in today’s edition. Subscribe by calling +248 4290999 or email us at sales@today.sc

stories.title: Chagossians Forcibly Displaced to Seychelles
stories.description: The Facebook publication characterizes Harold Wilson's authorization of the British Indian Ocean Territory on 8 November 1965 as the beginning of the forced removal of the Chagossian population. It says that over the following few years the population was forcibly transferred from the Chagos archipelago to Seychelles, and that the largest island was leased to the United States for a military base.

publications.title: an island for no one  #Mauritius #Chagossians #history #army
publications.text:
An Island for No One: the true story of the Chagos Islands, the British Indian Ocean Territory, and the secret behind Diego Garcia, one of the most strategic US military bases on Earth.

Imagine an island chain where nobody is allowed to live. Not because it is empty, but because Britain made it that way. In the 1960s, the United States wanted a military base on a territory with no population and no pressure for independence. Britain’s solution was to make the people who already lived there disappear from the legal record.

The Chagossians were a real society, with their own Creole language, their own food, their own homes, and families going back six to eight generations. They were forced onto boats and dumped in Mauritius and Seychelles with almost no support. Internal British Foreign Office documents show officials knew exactly what they were doing and wrote about maintaining “the fiction” that the islanders were not permanent residents.

In this video you will learn:

Why the British Indian Ocean Territory is not really British
How Britain depopulated the Chagos Islands and exiled the Chagossians
What the International Court of Justice ruled about the Chagos Archipelago
Why the UK and Mauritius handover deal is stuck in limbo
How a British judge declared the ban on living in the territory unlawful
Why Diego Garcia matters so much for US military power and B-2 bomber operations

Today the territory must be returned to Mauritius because the islanders’ right to self-determination was ignored in the past, yet it may not be returned because of those same rights today. Only a few hundred Chagossians who lived on the islands are still alive to see how it ends.

🔔 Subscribe to CHOKE THEORY for more untold history, geopolitics explained, and stories they never taught you in school. Turn on notifications so you never miss a new video.

#ChagosIslands #DiegoGarcia #Geopolitics #UntoldHistory #Shorts

On this day, 8 November 1965, Harold Wilson, the "socialist" Labour prime minister, authorised the establishment of the British Indian Ocean Territory. 
This was the first act in the ethnic cleansing of the Chagos archipelago. Over the next few years every member of the Chagossian population was forcibly removed from their home, never to return. 
One foreign office official wrote to diplomat Dennis Greenhill, saying: “We must surely be very tough about this. The object of the exercise was to get some rocks which will remain ours. There will be no Indigenous population except seagulls." Greenhill replied: "Along with the birds go some few Tarzans or Men Fridays". 
The Indigenous people were allowed to take just one suitcase each before being forcibly transferred to the Seychelles, and any pets were destroyed. 
The purpose of this ethnic cleansing was so that government could lease the largest island to the United States for $1 per year for them to establish a military base.
More information, sources and map: https://stories.workingclasshistory.com/article/10846/ethnic-cleansing-of-the-chagos-islands

He said the work needed to continue in preparation for the rainy season in December 2026.

stories.title: Seychelles Firefighters Complete Shipboard Firefighting Training
stories.description: From 28 September to 16 October 2026, two instructors from Marseille (France)’s naval fire battalion trained firefighters from the Seychelles Fire and Rescue Services Agency in responding to fires aboard ships. The three-week programme included theory, practical exercises aboard docked vessels, and training future trainers to support continued skills transfer.

publications.text:
🚒🚢 La coopération franco-seychelloise au service de la sécurité maritime !

Pendant trois semaines, du 28 septembre au 16 octobre 2026, deux instructeurs du Bataillon de marins-pompiers de Marseille (BMPM) ont partagé leur expertise avec les pompiers seychellois de la Seychelles Fire and Rescue Services Agency (SFRSA).

🎯 L’objectif ? Renforcer les capacités d’intervention des équipes seychelloises dans la lutte contre les incendies à bord des navires.

Au programme : enseignements théoriques, exercices pratiques à bord de navires à quai et partage d’expérience pour améliorer la sécurité et la coordination des interventions.

🤝 Une attention particulière a été portée à la formation de futurs formateurs, afin d’assurer une transmission durable des compétences.

👏 Bravo à tous les participants et merci aux formateurs et partenaires pour leur engagement !

Une belle illustration de la coopération concrète entre la France et les Seychelles, au service de la sécurité de tous. 🇫🇷🇸🇨

#LaFranceAuxSeychelles #CoopérationFrancoSeychelloise #SécuritéMaritime #MarinsPompiers

Certificate Presentation Ceremony – Ship Fire Fighting Training

The successful completion of Ship Fire Fighting Training Levels 1 and 2 marks an important achievement in strengthening Seychelles’ maritime emergency preparedness and capacity to respond effectively to shipboard fire incidents.

To commemorate this achievement, the Seychelles Fire and Rescue Services Agency (SFRSA) held a certificate presentation ceremony to recognise the participants who completed the training, as well as the instructors whose expertise and commitment continue to enhance professional firefighting capabilities. The training was delivered by trainers from the French cooperation, with the support of the Government of France, and brought together representatives from the Seychelles Fire and Rescue Services Agency, the Seychelles Coast Guard, the Seychelles Ports Authority and the Seychelles Maritime Safety Agency.

The programme enhanced practical skills, operational readiness and inter-agency cooperation in managing shipboard fire emergencies.

The ceremony was attended by the Ambassador of France to Seychelles, Mrs Anne Talineau; the Principal Secretary for Homeland Security, Ms Michelle Sabury; the Chief Fire Officer, Ms Tally Domingue; and representatives of the participating organisations.

Congratulations to all participants on their achievement, and sincere thanks to the trainers from the French cooperation and all partners for their valuable contributions to this important training initiative.

stories.title: Seychelles First Lady Presents Four-Year Social Strategy
stories.description: Véronique Herminie presented a four-year social strategy at State House (Seychelles) on 23 October 2026, aimed at strengthening community initiatives. The programme prioritises education, women’s empowerment, health and the wellbeing of vulnerable people, with implementation expected to rely on mobilising resources and partners. The publication says funding, selected projects and results will show whether the strategy translates into concrete action.

publications.text:
Seychelles : Véronique Herminie dévoile une stratégie sociale sur quatre ans

Les femmes, les enfants et les personnes vulnérables au cœur des priorités.

La Première dame des Seychelles, Véronique Herminie, a présenté le 23 octobre 2026, à State House, une stratégie sociale sur quatre ans visant à renforcer les initiatives communautaires.

Le programme met l’accent sur l’éducation, l’autonomisation des femmes, la santé et le bien-être des personnes vulnérables. Sa mise en œuvre reposera notamment sur la mobilisation de ressources et de partenaires.

Au-delà des annonces, le défi sera de traduire ces orientations en actions concrètes et mesurables. Les financements mobilisés, les projets retenus et les résultats obtenus permettront d’évaluer l’efficacité de cette stratégie.

L’enjeu : améliorer durablement les conditions de vie des populations les plus vulnérables.

Regards Citoyens Comores
Voir juste. Dire vrai. Servir l’intérêt.

De Maurice en passant par Madagascar et Mayotte, la presse met en avant les préoccupations du quotidien, les décisions attendues et les grands dossiers qui font réagir la population dans toute la région.

La Réunion : le futur aménagement du territoire fait débat

La Région Réunion prépare son schéma d’aménagement régional, un document stratégique qui orientera le développement de l’île à l’horizon 2050. Les enjeux concernent notamment le logement, l’agriculture et la préservation des milieux naturels. Ce projet suscite déjà des débats sur l’avenir et l’organisation du territoire réunionnais.

Le journal souligne également les défis du recrutement, avec beaucoup de candidats mais pas assez d’opportunités professionnelles.

Après les passes d’armes de la semaine dernière, la séance de ce mardi s’annonce électrique. Entre les questions sur les troubles, la gestion des fonds publics, les scandales présumés et les réformes annoncées, l’opposition et le gouvernement s’affrontent sur plusieurs dossiers sensibles. Une séance parlementaire sous haute tension, où chaque réponse sera scrutée.

Le chef de l’État, Michaël Randrianirina, se dit favorable au rétablissement du service national hors service militaire. Selon ses déclarations à Ihosy, les modalités de cette mesure sont encore à l’étude au niveau de l’Exécutif. L’objectif serait de renforcer chez les jeunes les valeurs de discipline, de responsabilité et de patriotisme, tout en favorisant leur engagement citoyen et leur insertion professionnelle.

Victoria Duthil raises concerns over Assomption development in ecocide law appeal

by H. Siu 

Seychellois marine biologist and environmental advocate Victoria Duthil has called for the recognition of ecocide as a serious crime under Seychelles law, arguing that the ongoing luxury resort development on Assomption Island has exposed significant weaknesses in the country's environmental protection and accountability mechanisms. The appeal was made in a guest blog titled ‘Our Crown Jewel, Their Luxury Hotel: Why Seychelles Needs 
Ecocide Law’, published on 16 October 2026 by Stop Ecocide International, an international non-profit organisation which advocates for the recognition of severe environmental destruction as a criminal offence worldwide.

stories.title: Nearly 10% of Seychelles Residents Reported Drug-Dependent
stories.description: The publication describes a heroin and crystal meth crisis in Seychelles and claims that nearly 10% of the population is dependent on one of the drugs. It characterizes this as a parallel society hidden from tourists; the supplied text provides no further support or detail for the estimate. The report was published on 6 November 2026.

publications.title: Drogen-Hotspot Seychellen: Wie Heroin und Crystal Meth das Urlaubsparadies verändern | Weltspiegel
publications.text:
Die Seychellen sind für Traumstrände, türkisblaues Meer und Luxusurlaub bekannt. Doch hinter dem Urlaubsparadies verbirgt sich ein großes Problem mit harten Drogen: Heroin, Crystal Meth und andere.

Einer, der etwas verändern will, ist Kenneth. Er arbeitet seit fast zehn Jahren als Sozialarbeiter für die Regierung. Kenneth war früher selbst abhängig. Heute unterstützt er Menschen beim Versuch, aus der Drogensucht herauszukommen. Auf seiner Tour über die Insel treffen wir Abhängige und einen Dealer und erleben eine Razzia der Polizei.
Wie konnte das Urlaubsparadies zum Drogen-Hotspot werden? Wie kommen die Drogen auf die Seychellen? Und kann Kenneth Menschen aus einer Sucht befreien, die er selbst nur zu gut kennt?

Autor: Karin Bensch
Kamera: Pascal Mörchen
Ton: Niclas Gonsior
Producer: Rassin Vannier, Patrick Gatua, Anne Fleischmann

stories.title: German Tourist Found Dead Near Anse Coco (Seychelles) Trail
stories.description: Seychelles Police reported that a German tourist was found dead near the Anse Coco (Seychelles) trail and that an investigation was launched. The date and circumstances of the death are not specified; the report was published on 28 October 2026.

publications.text:
🔴 𝐋𝐚𝐩𝐨𝐥𝐢𝐬 𝐈 𝐤𝐨𝐧𝐟𝐢𝐫𝐦 𝐥𝐚𝐧𝐦𝐨𝐫 𝐭𝐨𝐮𝐫𝐢𝐬 𝐀𝐥𝐦𝐚𝐧.

Dan en kominike lapolis I dir en lanket in konmanse pou etabli sirkonstans otour son lanmor an atandan rezilta letopsi.

Sa zonm Alman aze 30an, ti ariv Sesel le 25 Oktob 2026 e ti ekspekte kit pei demen le 28 Oktob 2026.

Police Statement (Follow-up) 🚨

The foreign visitor who was reported missing to the police this morning while hiking along the Anse Coco trail has been found dead this afternoon in an area off the trail between Petit Anse and Anse Coco.

The 30-year-old German national was reported missing after returning to Anse Coco beach at around 9 p.m. to retrieve diving equipment he had left behind earlier.

The police mobilised several officers from Mahé to assist with the search operation. These included officers from the Dog Unit, the Marine Police and the Drone Team, as well as officers from the Seychelles Fire and Rescue Services based on La Digue. Several civilians also assisted in the search.

A detailed investigation has been launched to establish the circumstances surrounding his death, pending the results of a post-mortem examination.

The visitor arrived in Seychelles on 25 October 2026 and was scheduled to leave the country on 28 October 2026.

stories.title: Seychelles Agencies Sign Blue Economy Data-Sharing MoUs
stories.description: On 10 November 2026, the Principal Secretary for the Blue Economy, the Seychelles Revenue Commission Commissioner General and the Registrar General signed two memoranda of understanding to improve the collection, exchange and analysis of data supporting the Blue Economy. The collaboration aims to strengthen evidence-based policymaking, statistical analysis and data systems, with information sharing subject to applicable legislation and data-protection safeguards.

publications.text:
SRC AND THE DEPARTMENT OF BLUE ECONOMY FORMALISE COOPERATION THROUGH SIGNING OF A MEMORANDUM OF UNDERSTANDING .

The Seychelles Revenue Commission and the Department of Blue Economy - Seychelles (DBE) have formalized their cooperation through the signing of a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU), establishing a framework for collaboration in areas of mutual interest, including information exchange, regulatory development and domestic revenue mobilization.

The MoU signed at the Department of Blue Economy on 10th November 2026 by the Principal Secretary of the Department of Blue Economy, Ms. Veronique Nibourette and the Acting Commissioner General of the Seychelles Revenue Commission, Mr. Fred Morel,  provides for the exchange of information and seeks to support the development and implementation of relevant frameworks for the Blue Economy, while strengthening cooperation in areas that contribute to domestic revenue mobilization.

Other areas of cooperation include joint awareness-raising initiatives, capacity-building activities in areas of specialized expertise and collaboration on matters of mutual interest.

STRENGTHENING DATA-DRIVEN DECISION-MAKING FOR SEYCHELLES’ BLUE ECONOMY

The Department of the Blue Economy, the Registration Division and the Seychelles Revenue Commission (SRC) today strengthened inter-institutional cooperation through two MOUs
 aimed at improving the collection, exchange and analysis of data to support the development of Seychelles’ Blue Economy.

The MoU was signed by the Principal Secretary for the Blue Economy, Ms. Veronique Nibourette, the Commissioner General of the Seychelles Revenue Commission, Mr.
Fred Morel, and the Registrar General, Mr. Suleiman Athanasius. Also present was the Secretary of State for Fisheries and Blue Economy, Mr. Alain de Comarmond.

The collaboration seeks to enhance the availability, quality and use of administrative and transactional data to support:

-Evidence-based policymaking: Strengthening the use of reliable data for policy formulation, planning and decision-making.
- Statistical analysis and forecasting: Improving the ability to analyse trends and support informed projections within thhe Blue Economy sector. 
- Improved data systems: Promoting better data collection, classifications, standards and statistical methodologies.
- Technical cooperation and capacity-building: Encouraging the exchange of expertise and institutional knowledge.

Through this partnership, the three institutions aim to share,  strengthen and improve the availability of information needed to guide the sustainable growth and development of Seychelles’ Blue Economy.

All information sharing will remain subject to applicable legislation, confidentiality requirements and appropriate data protection and information-security safeguards.

Better data. Stronger collaboration. More informed decisions for a sustainable Blue Economy.

Trending in science and nature right now: a tiny atoll in Seychelles is home to around 180,000 giant tortoises. That's more tortoises than there are people in the whole country. 🐢🏝️

A new survey of Aldabra giant tortoises on Aldabra Atoll, led by the Seychelles Islands Foundation (SIF) and the University of Exeter, estimated roughly 180,000 of them living there, the highest figure ever recorded for the species. The best estimate is almost 183,000 adult and sub-adult tortoises.

The team analysed five years of tortoise counts from 2018 to 2022. It's the first update since the widely cited figure of 100,000 from the late 1990s, and the study was published in the journal Ecology and Evolution.

Why it matters: in the 19th century, exploitation left fewer than 1,000 Aldabra tortoises on the island. A recovery programme followed, the atoll became a strict nature reserve in 1981 and a Unesco site in 1982, and researchers now call it one of the greatest conservation success stories of the Indian Ocean.

Aldabra is one of only two places in the world where giant tortoises live in the wild. The other is the Galápagos, with a much smaller population.

"More than 180,000 giant tortoises roaming freely on our atoll is proof of what long-term commitment to conservation can achieve," said Dr Frauke Fleischer-Dogley, CEO of SIF.

Counting them isn't easy either. Co-author Dr Nancy Bunbury said the atoll's dense vegetation makes it genuinely difficult, so the team modelled "what we didn't see, as well as what we did."

Still, the scientists say vigilance is essential: longer, more frequent droughts, rising sea levels, and invasive feral cats and black rats that prey on eggs and hatchlings remain threats. As Dr Dave Hudson put it, the numbers are "a baseline – not an endpoint."

Slow and steady really does win the race. 🐢

Source: The Guardian

🇸🇨 - Aldabra Atoll

Nearly 183,000 giant tortoises live on Aldabra Atoll in the Seychelles, according to a survey led by the Seychelles Islands Foundation and the University of Exeter. The population once fell below 1,000 after centuries of exploitation, but decades of protection have helped it recover. The latest estimate also exposes a hidden problem in wildlife conservation. A population that appears to have reached its limits may simply have been harder to count than expected. By accounting for animals missed during field surveys, researchers produced the first rigorous atoll-wide estimate in decades. Conservation depends not only on protecting wildlife, but also on measuring what survives accurately enough to guide future decisions.

🇸🇨 **Seychelles counts **[**record number of giant tortoises**](https://afrinz.ru/en/2026/10/seychelles-counts-record-number-of-giant-tortoises/) 

About 183,000 giant tortoises live on Aldabra Atoll in the Seychelles — this is the highest population estimate in the history of observations, reports the Seychelles Nation, citing an international study.

🔸Scientists from the Seychelles Islands Foundation and the University of Exeter in the UK analysed observation data collected on Aldabra between 2018 and 2022, and the results of their work were published in the scientific journal Ecology and Evolution. According to the researchers’ estimates, the population of giant tortoises on the atoll remains stable. Thus, Aldabra is home to the world’s largest population of these animals living in the wild.

🔸Previously, the Aldabra tortoise population was estimated at approximately 100,000 individuals. However, the scientists note that this does not indicate a sharp increase in the population over the past decades. The researchers hypothesize that previous counting methods failed to detect many tortoises that were hidden in the atoll’s dense vegetation.

🔸Scientists also noted that the situation is particularly significant in the context of Aldabra’s history. In the 19th century, due to mass hunting, the population of giant tortoises there dwindled to fewer than 1,000 individuals. Today, the atoll is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and remains one of the most important natural sites in the Seychelles.

Environ 183 000 tortues géantes vivent sur l’atoll d’Aldabra, aux Seychelles — l’estimation la plus élevée de l’effectif de cette population depuis le début des observations, rapporte le journal Seychelles Nation, citant une étude internationale.

Des chercheurs de la Seychelles Islands Foundation et de l’université britannique d’Exeter ont analysé les données d’observation recueillies à Aldabra entre 2018 et 2022, et les résultats de ces travaux ont été publiés dans la revue scientifique Ecology and Evolution. Selon les chercheurs, la population de tortues géantes de l’atoll reste stable. Aldabra abrite ainsi la plus grande population au monde de ces animaux vivant en milieu naturel.

🔶 L’effectif des tortues d’Aldabra était auparavant estimé à environ 100 000 individus. Les scientifiques relèvent toutefois que cela ne signifie pas une forte croissance de la population au cours des dernières décennies. Ils supposent que les méthodes de comptage antérieures ne permettaient pas de repérer de nombreuses tortues dissimulées dans la végétation dense de l’atoll.

Noticias eXplora:Las tortugas gigantes superan en número a las personas en Seychelles, con casi 183.000 en Aldabra [Las tortugas gigantes superan en número a las personas en Seychelles, con casi 183.000 en Aldabra ](https://i.blogs.es/5e18e8/mas-tortugas-que-personas-en-seychelles-a/1024_2000.jpeg) En el siglo XIX, la explotación sin freno dejó a las tortugas gigantes de Aldabra por debajo de los 1.000 ejemplares. Entre 2018 y 2021, ese mismo atolón de Seychelles albergaba casi 183.000, la cifra más alta jamás registrada para la especie y bastante más que los [cerca de 120.000 habitantes del país](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/POPTOTSCA647NWDB). Es el resultado del primer recuento riguroso de todo el atolón, y si lo traducimos a escala doméstica, salen a tres tortugas por cada dos habitantes del archip seychellenses.Las cifras. El trabajo, que firman Lara B. Hillyard y otros nueve investigadores de la Fundación de las Islas Seychelles (SIF, por sus siglas en inglés) y de la Universidad de Exeter, [analiza los conteos de 2018 a 2022](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/ece3.74282) y, con las cuatro primeras temporadas, las más completas, llega a una media de casi 183.000 tortugas adultas y subadultas, con una población estable durante todo ese tiempo. Es la mayor población de tortugas gigantes en libertad del planeta, y Aldabra es uno de los dos únicos lugares donde viven en estado salvaje, siendo el otro las Galápagos, aunque con bastantes menos ejemplares.La directora ejecutiva de la fundación y coautora del trabajo, Frauke Fleischer-Dogley, señala que "los datos de seguimiento de este estudio los recogió el personal de la SIF que vive y trabaja en el atolón, año tras año", y añade que "Más de 180.000 tortugas gigantes campando libremente por nuestro atolón son la prueba de lo que puede lograr un compromiso a largo plazo con la conservación". Un compromiso que quedó blindado en 1981, cuando Aldabra se convirtió en reserva natural estricta, para un año después ser declarado patrimonio de la humanidad por la UNESCO. [ Durante siglos, los marineros británicos devoraron a las tortugas verdes hasta casi extinguirlas: hoy las hemos recuperado ](https://www.xataka.com/ecologia-y-naturaleza/estuvieron-al-borde-desaparicion-moda-culinaria-britanica-hoy-tortugas-verdes-fin-estan-fuera-peligro) [En Xataka](https://www.xataka.com/ecologia-y-naturaleza/estuvieron-al-borde-desaparicion-moda-culinaria-britanica-hoy-tortugas-verdes-fin-estan-fuera-peligro) [Durante siglos, los marineros británicos devoraron a las tortugas verdes hasta casi extinguirlas: hoy las hemos recuperado](https://www.xataka.com/ecologia-y-naturaleza/estuvieron-al-borde-desaparicion-moda-culinaria-britanica-hoy-tortugas-verdes-fin-estan-fuera-peligro) ¿Se han duplicado? No es que se hayan doblado, pero la cifra más citada hasta ahora, de finales de los años noventa, rondaba los 100.000 ejemplares, aunque los autores advierten de que el salto no equivale a que la población se haya multiplicado de esa forma: los censos anteriores no tenían en cuenta a los animales que estaban ahí y nadie veía, así que muy probablemente se quedaban cortos. Otra de las coautoras del estudio, Nancy Bunbury, explica que "el programa de seguimiento de las tortugas gigantes de Aldabra es uno de los más longevos de la región, pero la densa vegetación del atolón hace que contarlas sea francamente difícil en algunos lugares".La forma de contabilizarlas aunque no se puedan ver como tal es con una técnica llamada muestreo por distancias. Dos observadores recorren a pie 17 itinerarios fijos una vez por estación húmeda y anotan cada tortuga y a qué distancia de su camino está. Cuanto más lejos y más tupida la vegetación, menos tortugas se ven, así que el modelo estadístico calcula esa pérdida en cada tipo de hábitat y rellena el hueco. Las mayores densidades salen en los herbazales que los investigadores llaman "tortoise turf" (algo así como césped de tortuga), y los escondites, en el matorral denso y los manglares. No obstante hay que señalar que las crías, muy esquivas, ni siquiera entran en la cuenta.Del borde al récord. La historia de los recuentos es más enrevesada de lo que sugiere el paso de 100.000 a 183.000. En 1978, los investigadores Bourn y Coe ya habían estimado unas 150.000 tortugas en todo el atolón, aunque sin corregir por los animales que no se veían (justo lo que aporta el nuevo modelo), y la revisión de 1997, que era más ligera, bajó a esos 100.000. El nuevo trabajo concluye que ambas cifras se quedaban cortas y desmonta la idea -que se dio por buena durante años- de que a finales del siglo XX la población había tocado techo. FROM 1,000 TO 180,000: THE UNBELIEVABLE COMEBACK OF SEYCHELLES' GIANT TORTOISES

Once hunted to near-extinction, giant tortoises in the Seychelles have made a stunning comeback—now outnumbering humans by the tens of thousands. A recent survey reveals that over 180,000 Aldabra giant tortoises roam the uninhabited Aldabra Atoll, up from just 1,000 in the late 19th century. This is the kind of environmental news we need more of! The full story on how they pulled this off is here: https://geni.us/CBS-NEWS

Aldabra Atoll is a ring of coral islands in the far southwest of the Seychelles, remote enough that few people have ever set foot on it. In the 1800s it wasn't remote enough, and hunting reduced its giant tortoises to fewer than 1,000 animals.

Giant tortoises were prized by sailors because they could be kept alive aboard ship for long periods without food or water. That made them a source of fresh meat on long voyages and drove their collapse on islands across the Indian Ocean.

Aldabra became a strict nature reserve in 1981, and the tortoises have been left almost entirely alone since then. A new count by the Seychelles Islands Foundation and the University of Exeter, published in Ecology and Evolution, puts the population at about 180,000. That's the highest figure ever recorded and more than the 122,000 people who live in the whole country.

The researchers describe the number as a modeled estimate rather than an individual count, and the atoll's future still depends on things protection can't control, from drought to rising seas. On the islands where hunting almost ended them, the tortoises now outnumber the citizens of the nation that owns them.

#curiousminds

There are more giant tortoises on one Seychelles atoll than there are people in the whole of Seychelles.

A new survey of Aldabra Atoll has counted roughly 180,000 Aldabra giant tortoises roaming free the highest figure ever recorded for the species. The last widely cited number, from the late 1990s, was 100,000.

Aldabra is one of only two places on Earth where giant tortoises still live in the wild. The other is the Galápagos, where the population is much smaller.

In the 19th century, after decades of exploitation, fewer than 1,000 were left on the atoll. A recovery programme followed. Aldabra became a strict nature reserve in 1981 and a UNESCO site the year after, and the tortoises were left alone.

“More than 180,000 giant tortoises roaming freely on our atoll is proof of what long-term commitment to conservation can achieve,” said Dr Frauke Fleischer-Dogley of the Seychelles Islands Foundation, which led the survey with the University of Exeter.

The count took five years of fieldwork, from 2018 to 2022. Aldabra’s vegetation is dense enough that counting tortoises is genuinely difficult, so the team modelled the ones they couldn’t see as well as the ones they could.

The researchers call it a baseline rather than a finish line. Droughts are getting longer, sea levels are rising on low-lying ground, and feral cats and black rats still take tortoise eggs and hatchlings. Clearing those out, they say, could remove the last thing holding the population back.

A survey led by the Seychelles Islands Foundation (SIF) and the University of Exeter revealed there were about 180,000 Aldabra giant tortoises living on the island.

The new figure was obtained by a team who analysed five years of tortoise counts between 2018 and 2022. It is the first update since a widely cited figure of 100,000 tortoises from the late 1990s.

Researchers are now saying it is one of the greatest conservation success stories of the Indian Ocean, with the new study confirming it.

Despite the good news, the study’s authors say that vigilance is essential. Aldabra’s climate is changing, with longer and more frequent droughts predicted to reduce the shade and food available to tortoises, while rising sea levels threaten low-lying parts of the atoll.

publications.title: Seychelles Island Now Has 183,000 Giant Tortoises — More Than the Country's Entire Population
publications.text:
A new study led by the Seychelles Islands Foundation and the University of Exeter has revealed that Aldabra Atoll in Seychelles is home to approximately 183,000 adult and sub-adult Aldabra giant tortoises, the largest known population of free-roaming giant tortoises in the world. 

The findings, published in the journal Ecology and Evolution, mark the first rigorous atoll-wide estimate since the widely cited figure of 100,000 from the late 1990s.

Researchers analysed five years of tortoise counts collected between 2018 and 2022 and used a statistical modelling technique to account for animals hidden in dense scrub and other hard-to-survey habitats. 

The estimate exceeds the Seychelles human population, recorded at 123,565 by the National Bureau of Statistics as of June 2026.

In the 19th century, exploitation reduced the Aldabra giant tortoise population to fewer than 1,000 individuals. 

Aldabra became a strict nature reserve in 1981 and a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1982, after which the population gradually recovered. 

Despite the positive numbers, the study's authors caution that longer and more frequent droughts are expected to reduce food and shade, rising sea levels threaten low-lying areas of the atoll, and invasive feral cats and black rats continue to prey on tortoise eggs and hatchlings.

publications.title: Aldabra Giant Tortoise Species Makes a Comeback🐢
publications.text:
The Aldabra giant tortoise is one of the most remarkable examples of wildlife conservation in the Indian Ocean. Native to Aldabra Atoll in the Seychelles, these enormous reptiles live in a protected island ecosystem where their grazing, movement, and seed dispersal help shape the surrounding environment.

For centuries, giant tortoises across the Indian Ocean were heavily exploited by sailors and settlers for food. Hunting and habitat changes caused populations on many islands to disappear, leaving Aldabra as one of the last major strongholds for giant tortoises in the region.

Aldabra’s long-term survival was helped by conservation efforts that protected the atoll from extensive development and exploitation. The site became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1982, recognizing its exceptional natural value and the importance of preserving its unique wildlife.

A scientific study published in 2026 estimated that approximately 180,000 Aldabra giant tortoises live on Aldabra Atoll. Researchers from the Seychelles Islands Foundation and the University of Exeter contributed to the research, which provides a more comprehensive population estimate than earlier surveys. The tortoises now outnumber the human population of the entire Seychelles nation.

The Aldabra giant tortoise, scientifically known as Aldabrachelys gigantea, is one of the world's largest tortoise species. During the 19th century, intensive hunting for meat and other resources devastated giant tortoise populations across the Indian Ocean, leaving Aldabra as their last major natural stronghold in the region.

By the late 1800s, fewer than 1,000 tortoises may have remained on Aldabra. Conservation efforts gradually reduced human exploitation, allowing the population to recover. The atoll's designation as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1982 further strengthened protections for its unique ecosystem.

To produce the new estimate, researchers analyzed tortoise monitoring data collected by field teams between 2018 and 2022. Their statistical models accounted for differences in habitat and the likelihood of tortoises being overlooked during surveys. The study appeared in the scientific journal Ecology and Evolution.

The new estimate does not necessarily mean the population nearly doubled in recent decades. Earlier surveys estimated around 100,000 tortoises, but researchers believe those methods may have missed animals hidden in dense vegetation or shaded areas. The latest research provides a more reliable picture of a population that appears to have remained relatively stable during the study period.

Aldabra's giant tortoises also play an important ecological role. As large herbivores, they graze on vegetation, create pathways through the landscape, and disperse seeds. These activities help shape the atoll's habitats and influence the other species living there.

Despite their impressive numbers, the tortoises remain vulnerable because their principal wild population is concentrated on one remote atoll. Climate change, rising sea levels, and extreme weather could threaten their habitat in the future. Continued monitoring and conservation management will be important to protect the population.

The discovery demonstrates the value of long-term habitat protection and improved scientific monitoring. Aldabra's giant tortoises have survived centuries of human exploitation, and the latest research shows how sustained conservation can help preserve one of the world's most extraordinary wildlife populations.

🐢 1. Landmark Wildlife Discovery: Aldabra Giant Tortoise Population Reaches ~183,000
The Story: A comprehensive study published by the Seychelles Islands Foundation (SIF) and the University of Exeter revealed that Aldabra Atoll now hosts nearly 183,000 giant tortoises.

Why it matters: This historic baseline means the giant tortoise population on the remote UNESCO World Heritage Site officially outnumbers the entire human population of Seychelles.

#seychelles #NewsAlert

More than 180,000 giant tortoises now roam a remote island paradise in the Indian Ocean. Their ancestors came dangerously close to extinction, but decades of conservation have helped turn their survival into one of the most remarkable wildlife recovery stories in the world.

Located in the Seychelles, Aldabra Atoll is home to the world's largest free-roaming population of giant tortoises. These enormous reptiles, scientifically known as Aldabrachelys gigantea, are among the last surviving giant tortoise populations on Earth.

Their history, however, was not always so promising. During the 18th and 19th centuries, sailors and traders heavily exploited giant tortoises for food, often collecting them in large numbers and transporting them aboard ships. By the end of the 19th century, hunting had reduced Aldabra's population to fewer than 1,000 individuals.

Fortunately, stronger conservation measures helped protect the remaining animals and their habitat. Aldabra received strict nature reserve protection in 1981 and was recognized as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1982.

In October 2026, researchers from the University of Exeter and the Seychelles Islands Foundation announced a new scientific estimate of approximately 182,424 adult and sub-adult tortoises. The research analyzed years of population monitoring data collected between 2018 and 2022.

Interestingly, scientists explained that earlier estimates had probably missed many tortoises hiding in dense vegetation. This means the new figure does not represent a sudden population explosion, but rather a more accurate assessment of how many animals actually live there.

Beyond their impressive numbers, these ancient reptiles play an essential role in their ecosystem. They graze on vegetation, disperse seeds, and influence the growth of plants across the islands, helping maintain the natural balance of their habitat.

Despite their recovery, climate change, prolonged droughts, rising sea levels, and invasive predators continue to threaten their long-term survival.

Aldabra's giant tortoises demonstrate how sustained conservation and scientific monitoring can protect wildlife for generations.

One of the most remarkable wildlife conservation stories comes from the Seychelles, where giant tortoises have recovered from the brink of extinction after more than a century of protection.

In the late 1800s, the population of Aldabra giant tortoises had fallen dramatically, with historical estimates suggesting that only around 1,000 individuals remained.

These enormous reptiles were once widespread across islands in the Indian Ocean. However, centuries of hunting, habitat destruction, and exploitation by sailors caused devastating population declines.

Today, the Aldabra Atoll in Seychelles supports one of the world’s largest populations of giant tortoises, with estimates reaching approximately 100,000 individuals. Higher figures sometimes refer to broader population estimates, but the exact number varies between surveys.

Aldabra is a remote coral atoll that has remained relatively undisturbed by large-scale human development. Its isolation, combined with strict conservation measures, has allowed the tortoises to reproduce and recover naturally.

These animals are among the largest tortoises on Earth. Adult males can weigh more than 200 kilograms, and individuals can survive for well over a century.

Their ecological importance extends beyond their impressive size. Giant tortoises act as ecosystem engineers, grazing vegetation, dispersing seeds, and helping shape the landscapes they inhabit.

As they move across the islands, they influence plant growth and create conditions that support other species.

The Aldabra Atoll was designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in recognition of its exceptional biodiversity and ecological importance.

The recovery of these tortoises demonstrates what sustained conservation efforts can achieve when habitats are protected and human pressures are reduced.

At a time when biodiversity loss is accelerating worldwide, their survival offers an important example of how species can recover when given sufficient protection.

Researchers just tallied a whopping nearly 183,000 giant tortoises on one remote Seychelles island, an absolute army of them that now outnumbers every single human in the entire country.

Yes, the slow, tank sized reptiles currently have a bigger population than the humans of Seychelles. After being hunted down to fewer than 1,000 in the 1800s, the Aldabra giant tortoises pulled off a comeback so successful that the latest rigorous survey puts the number of adults and near-adults at nearly 183,000. Decades of strict protection (nature reserve since 1981, UNESCO site since 1982) did the heavy lifting. Earlier estimates of 100,000 were basically undercounts because a lot of them were just chilling in the bushes where surveyors couldn’t see them.

The population looks stable, not exploding overnight. They’re still the world’s largest free roaming giant tortoise herd, living on a remote coral atoll basically left alone by people. 

Droughts, rising seas, and invasive rats and cats could still mess things up, but for now the tortoises are quietly winning at the whole “outnumber the locals” thing.

There are more giant tortoises on one Seychelles island than people in the entire country.

Scientists from the Seychelles Islands Foundation and the University of Exeter counted roughly 180,000 of them on Aldabra Atoll, a lost world almost nobody gets to visit. The whole Seychelles has about 123,000 humans.

Here's the wild part. In the 19th century, hunting left fewer than 1,000 of these animals alive. 

Then people backed off. The atoll was shielded from human influence, and the tortoises just kept quietly multiplying. The last big estimate, from the late 1990s, was 100,000. 

Now it's closer to double that.

Slow and steady actually won.

There are now thought to be one hundred and eighty three thousand of them, and about four hundred and forty five of us a year.

A study by the Seychelles Islands Foundation and the University of Exeter, announced this month, puts the giant tortoise population of Aldabra at almost one hundred and eighty three thousand adults and sub adults, roughly double the figure that had stood since the late nineties. In the nineteenth century exploitation had taken them below one thousand. The atoll became a strict nature reserve in 1981 and a World Heritage site in 1982, and feral goats were cleared in 2012. There is no airstrip, no harbour and no jetty. Every visitor arrives by live aboard with permission and is accompanied throughout.

Some protection looks like a place being left almost entirely alone.

Journey Further, Bond Deeply ✨

.

#MosaicoCollective #JourneyFurtherBondDeeply #Seychelles #Aldabra #WorldHeritage

Photo: Cedric Fox

Aldabra Atoll in the Seychelles may now be home to roughly 180,000 giant tortoises, according to scientists, and that number is a rare bit of good conservation news. Back in the 1800s, their numbers had been pushed below 1,000 animals. After long-term protection, the same population has climbed back in a way that feels genuinely remarkable. The new estimate is not a quick guess from a beach walk. Researchers used five years of monitoring, then paired the field data with statistical modelling so tortoises missed in thick vegetation were still accounted for. That makes this the strongest count yet.
